content.content:
1	# A write socket is a strata writer's presence
     2	
     3	Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.
     4	
     5	## Decision
     6	
     7	An editor holds a durable strata writer through one WebSocket,
     8	`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/strata/{store}/sockets`. The writer is created when
     9	the socket opens and evicted when it closes, so the connection is the writer's
    10	presence. Edits arrive on it as records operations and are acknowledged on it;
    11	what other writers do after the editor's read (`?changes_token=`) leaves on it as patches
    12	and records, read the way the records changes stream reads them (ADR 0009),
    13	without the records only this writer touched.
    14	
    15	One-shot writes (`POST …/edits`) stay plain HTTP: each is its own writer,
    16	announced, written and evicted in one ref transaction, with no presence to hold.
    17	
    18	## Why a WebSocket, not SSE
    19	
    20	This is a documented exception to PUBLIC-STREAM-001, which asks for server push
    21	over SSE. The socket is not a push channel with writes beside it; it is one
    22	session, and splitting it into an SSE stream plus POSTs would lose what the
    23	session is for:
    24	
    25	- **Presence needs one connection.** A strata writer holds back compaction until
    26	  it is evicted, so its lifetime has to end when the editor leaves. With SSE plus
    27	  POSTs, no single connection's end says the editor left: a POST can arrive after
    28	  the stream dropped, on another replica, for a writer nobody holds any more.
    29	- **One writer, one owner.** The writer's store is single-threaded, and the socket
    30	  is the goroutine that owns it. POSTs would arrive on any replica and need the
    31	  writer handed between them.
    32	- **Ordering.** Frames on one socket are applied in order and acknowledged by
    33	  sequence number. Independent POSTs would need ordering rebuilt on top.
    34	
    35	On reconnect a client opens a new socket, as a new writer, and passes as `changes_token`
    36	the token of the state it last holds; that is the outbound half's resume. The
    37	rule does not require one on an ephemeral stream, but a token makes it free.
    38	
    39	## Presence and cleanup
    40	
    41	- **Lease.** A writer's lease row is taken before it announces itself and renewed
    42	  while the socket is open. A writer whose renewal lapses fences itself, refuses
    43	  further edits and closes the socket.
    44	- **Crash backstop.** A replica that dies leaves its writers' leases to lapse. The
    45	  next session on the store evicts lapsed writers, folds and retires them; there
    46	  is no background sweeper.
    47	- **Failed starts keep the lease.** Once the lease is taken the writer may already
    48	  be announced, and only a leased writer can be evicted later.
    49	
    50	## Authority
    51	
    52	- Opening a socket and writing need `push` on the repo; creating a store needs
    53	  `manage_settings`.
    54	- Every git operation, maintenance included, runs on the caller's bearer. So any
    55	  pusher can evict any lapsed writer; there is no entiredb carve-out.
    56	- The bearer is re-checked every minute, and the socket ends before it expires,
    57	  because ending the writer needs it.
    58	
    59	## Placement
    60	
    61	Strata writes are git pushes, which may enter at any placement that holds the
    62	repo (PUBLIC-CELL-003's exception). Both the socket and the one-shot routes admit
    63	on every cell, not only the processing primary.
    64	
    65	## Consequences
    66	
    67	- A client keeps each edit until a read shows it, and sends it again after
    68	  reconnecting, so edits must be safe to repeat. The published app's are: an
    69	  edit that already landed is a no-op.
    70	- Any pusher can end another person's lapsed writer. That is the price of having
    71	  no service-side authority over strata refs.
     1	# A records read continues as a stream of changes
     2	
     3	Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.
     4	
     5	## Context
     6	
     7	A records client that follows a store live has had one tool: watch the ref-event
     8	stream for the store's refs and read the collections again whole whenever one
     9	moves. The published planning app does exactly that, and while someone types it
    10	re-reads the whole store about once a commit, in every open tab. The store is
    11	small, so each read is cheap, but the rate is the commit rate times the number
    12	of viewers, and every read ships every record to tell the reader about one.
    13	
    14	The write socket already reports changes (ADR 0008), but only to an editor: a
    15	socket is a writer, so it needs `push`, holds a lease and counts against the
    16	replica's cap, and it leaves out its own writer's edits. A viewer has none of
    17	those to spend and needs every writer's edits.
    18	
    19	## Decision
    20	
    21	**`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records/{schema}/changes` streams what a store does
    22	after a state the caller has read.** Server-sent events, gated like every
    23	records read (`pull`).
    24	
    25	- A collections read returns `changesToken` with its records. The stream starts
    26	  from it (`?changes_token=`): not `since`, which this API's other operations
    27	  use for RFC 3339 time bounds, and snake_case as RFD-026 asks of new
    28	  parameters (the older records routes' camelCase is grandfathered).
    29	- Each time the store's refs move, the stream reads what changed since the last
    30	  state it reported and sends a `changed` event: what changed in records the
    31	  caller holds, the records it cannot hold yet, and the ones that are gone. Its
    32	  `id` is a token for the state they were read at,
    33	  so an EventSource that reconnects resumes from `Last-Event-ID`, which is
    34	  PUBLIC-STREAM-001's resume with the state as the thing resumed.
    35	- `ready` marks the stream live. It ends with `reconnect` after a bounded time,
    36	  and `forbidden` when access goes, like the other streams.
    37	
    38	**What changed is read from the projection, not taken from the event.** The
    39	ref-event hub is only the doorbell, as it is for the write socket. Every answer
    40	catches the projection up first, like every records read, so a ring that lands
    41	mid-read is answered by the next one and nothing falls between two.
    42	
    43	**A record the caller holds comes back as a patch, decided and decoded here.**
    44	The changed rows already say which fields moved, and a list's entries are rows of
    45	their own, so a patch carries each changed field's value as the collections read
    46	shapes it, or, for a list that only grew at its end, just the new entries and the
    47	length the list now has. One keystroke into a body is one entry. Which changed
    48	fields are entries pushed at a list's end is entire-records' to say
    49	(`Snapshot.GetRecordChange`), from the same read that fetches the record and by
    50	entry rather than by value, so no layout is taken apart here. Label, parent and
    51	rank are restated whole. Anything an append cannot say, such as a fold removing
    52	entries, sends that field whole. A record is held when one of its visible fields
    53	predates the token and its delete floor has not risen since; anything else comes
    54	back whole.
    55	
    56	Not strata's ops. An op is undecided (many lose), and deciding it is
    57	`record.Supersedes` plus delete floors, expiry and erasure; reading it as a
    58	record is entire-records' decode. A browser doing both would be a third
    59	implementation of the rules the projection's conformance cases and ADR 0005 exist
    60	to keep in one place, and it would need every field's stamp, which no read
    61	returns. The rows are the ops after they were decided, so a patch is about the
    62	size of the op that caused it.
    63	
    64	**A projection numbers its ticks, and each row records the tick that last wrote
    65	it.** "What changed since a state" is then the rows whose tick is past the
    66	state's. Ticks of one store are serialised by its advisory lock, so the numbers
    67	commit in order. A tick that writes no row takes no number.
    68	
    69	The per-writer cursor would also answer the question, exactly, but it grows with
    70	every writer that has ever written to the store (one per editing session), and a
    71	token carrying it would outgrow the header it has to travel in. A tick number
    72	does not grow.
    73	
    74	**The token is small and opaque:** generation, tick, schema version, and a digest
    75	of the store's expiry and erasure sets. A row is only rewritten when its value is
    76	superseded, so an unchanged tick means nothing a reader holds has moved.
    77	
    78	**When a change cannot be told as records, the stream says `reload` and ends.**
    79	That covers a new generation, a schema version the token did not read, a
    80	projection behind the token, and an expiry or erasure (they delete rows rather
    81	than write them, so no tick names what they took). The client reads the
    82	collections again and opens a new stream from that read's token. A reload carries
    83	no `id`, so an EventSource that reconnects anyway resumes from the last good
    84	token and is told again.
    85	
    86	**The write socket tells its editor the same way.** It takes the changesToken
    87	of the read the editor's page made (`?changes_token=`, refused when this service did not
    88	issue it) and, at once and then on each ring, reads what changed since with this
    89	stream's read, less the records only its own writer touched: each projection row
    90	names the writer that decided it. A ring that moved only its own writer's log is
    91	its own write coming back, and is not read. Editors get patches too, and one set
    92	of reload rules covers both. The writer's own feed cursor, which the socket used
    93	to answer from, is gone. A socket opened without `changes_token` reports no changes.
    94	
    95	## Consequences
    96	
    97	- A viewer following a store pays one small event per commit instead of a whole
    98	  read, and an editor's edits reach the viewer the same way as anyone else's.
    99	- The length in an append is the caller's check that it applied every earlier
   100	  event. Two writers pushing the same value in the same millisecond write one
   101	  entry twice; the second reads as an append of an entry the caller holds, the
   102	  lengths disagree, and the caller reads again.
   103	- Each ring still costs a catch-up per stream, under the store's lock. *Amended
   104	  2026-10-13:* it used to be a whole fetch each — a fresh clone takes the store
   105	  with no haves — and every stream but the first found nothing new. Testing the
   106	  planning store, that was about 1,300 full fetches in a day and a half, ~1 MB
   107	  each and growing, against ~200 one-shot reads: the rings were the cost. A tick
   108	  now keeps where its read stopped (strata's `Since`, in the cursor's `tips`):
   109	  a ring costs an ls-refs for every stream that finds the store unmoved, and one
   110	  fetch of only the new log entries for the one that does not. A new generation
   111	  is still read whole. Measured on the same store, a push went from ~3 MB of
   112	  fetches to ~4 KB. `records.read` on the request span says which read a tick
   113	  took; if the lock wait shows up (`records.lock_wait_ms`), the hub can catch
   114	  the store up once per ring and fan out.
   115	- A changes read scans one store's rows by the primary key's prefix. `tick` is
   116	  not indexed, because an indexed column makes every update non-HOT (the reason
   117	  `repo_record_fields_fact_idx` leaves `lamport` out). For stores of a few
   118	  thousand rows that is the right trade; a large store would want the index.
   119	- Nested records are reported by their own address, as the write socket reports
   120	  them.
   121	- `tip` does not cover the expiry set, so two states that differ only in expired
   122	  facts share a tip. The changes token covers it; the tip is unchanged here.
   123	
   124	## Amendment, 2026-10-14: the doorbell is not debounced
   125	
   126	The ref-event hub debounces each ref for 200 ms before delivering, which suits
   127	`/refs/events`, where every event becomes a frame per viewer. A stream or socket
   128	only reads what moved, and its one-slot wake already folds a burst into one read,
   129	so the window added 200 ms to every change and saved nothing: each writer pushes
   130	its own log ref, and its pushes are a second or more apart. Nor did it merge
   131	several writers' pushes: the window is per ref, so a burst across refs flushed
   132	200 ms later with the spacing it arrived with, and only the wake ever folded it.
   133	Both now join the hub as doorbells, rung as the event arrives; `/refs/events`
   134	keeps the debounce.
   135	`records.ring_lag` measures a ring from entiredb stamping its oldest event to the
   136	read it rang being answered, by consumer and outcome.

     3	Status: accepted, 2026-10-12.
     4	
     5	## Decision
     6	
     7	An editor holds a durable strata writer through one WebSocket,
     8	`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/strata/{store}/sockets`. The writer is created when
     9	the socket opens and evicted when it closes, so the connection is the writer's
    10	presence. Edits arrive on it as records operations and are acknowledged on it;
    11	what other writers do after the editor's read (`?changes_token=`) leaves on it as patches
    12	and records, read the way the records changes stream reads them (ADR 0009),
    13	without the records only this writer touched.
    14	
    15	One-shot writes (`POST …/edits`) stay plain HTTP: each is its own writer,
    16	announced, written and evicted in one ref transaction, with no presence to hold.
    17	
    18	## Why a WebSocket, not SSE
    19	
    20	This is a documented exception to PUBLIC-STREAM-001, which asks for server push
    21	over SSE. The socket is not a push channel with writes beside it; it is one
    22	session, and splitting it into an SSE stream plus POSTs would lose what the
    23	session is for:
    24	
    25	- **Presence needs one connection.** A strata writer holds back compaction until
    26	  it is evicted, so its lifetime has to end when the editor leaves. With SSE plus
    27	  POSTs, no single connection's end says the editor left: a POST can arrive after
    28	  the stream dropped, on another replica, for a writer nobody holds any more.
    29	- **One writer, one owner.** The writer's store is single-threaded, and the socket
    30	  is the goroutine that owns it. POSTs would arrive on any replica and need the
    31	  writer handed between them.
    32	- **Ordering.** Frames on one socket are applied in order and acknowledged by
    33	  sequence number. Independent POSTs would need ordering rebuilt on top.
    34	
    35	On reconnect a client opens a new socket, as a new writer, and passes as `changes_token`
    36	the token of the state it last holds; that is the outbound half's resume. The
    37	rule does not require one on an ephemeral stream, but a token makes it free.
    38	
    39	## Presence and cleanup
    40	
    41	- **Lease.** A writer's lease row is taken before it announces itself and renewed
    42	  while the socket is open. A writer whose renewal lapses fences itself, refuses
    43	  further edits and closes the socket.
    44	- **Crash backstop.** A replica that dies leaves its writers' leases to lapse. The
    45	  next session on the store evicts lapsed writers, folds and retires them; there
    46	  is no background sweeper.
    47	- **Failed starts keep the lease.** Once the lease is taken the writer may already
    48	  be announced, and only a leased writer can be evicted later.
    49	
    50	## Authority
    51	
    52	- Opening a socket and writing need `push` on the repo; creating a store needs
    53	  `manage_settings`.
    54	- Every git operation, maintenance included, runs on the caller's bearer. So any
    55	  pusher can evict any lapsed writer; there is no entiredb carve-out.
    56	- The bearer is re-checked every minute, and the socket ends before it expires,
    57	  because ending the writer needs it.
    58

    60	
    61	Strata writes are git pushes, which may enter at any placement that holds the
    62	repo (PUBLIC-CELL-003's exception). Both the socket and the one-shot routes admit
    63	on every cell, not only the processing primary.
    64

    66	
    67	- A client keeps each edit until a read shows it, and sends it again after
    68	  reconnecting, so edits must be safe to repeat. The published app's are: an
    69	  edit that already landed is a no-op.
    70	- Any pusher can end another person's lapsed writer. That is the price of having
    71	  no service-side authority over strata refs.

1	# Records are read through entire-records' own decode
     2	
     3	Status: accepted, 2026-08-10; amended 2026-10-01 (records move to the v0 surface); amended 2026-10-10 (reads come from strata)
     4	
     5	## Context
     6	
     7	A repo can hold [entire-records](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-records)
     8	stores: schema-described structured data kept as git trees on
     9	`refs/meta/records/<schema>/main`. Until now this service served only the raw
    10	`(target, key, value)` triples, on `GET /repos/{id}/meta/targets`, leaving every
    11	consumer to decode them.
    12	
    13	Decoding is not a formatting step. The rules are not recoverable by looking at the
    14	data: a record's shard is a hash of its id rather than an id prefix, a field's
    15	`:type` and `:value` keys recombine into one value, keys no type declares are
    16	dropped, an absent set encodes as `[]` where an absent scalar encodes as `null`,
    17	and an ordered type's records are sorted by a rank field. A second implementation
    18	gets most of that right and produces plausible-looking wrong records — which is
    19	worse than failing.
    20	
    21	entire-records' ADR `20260803-records-become-a-cell-api-concept` decided the
    22	answer jointly with us: records become a concept of this service, and that repo
    23	supplies the decode as a library above a two-method read seam (`store.Reader`).
    24	entire.io's TypeScript app then fetches decoded records over one hop and contains
    25	no records logic, which is what "no Go in that app" was asking for.
    26	
    27	## Decision
    28	
    29	**`internal/records` implements those two methods over this cell's git data plane,
    30	and imports everything above them.** It is the third implementation of the seam —
    31	a clone on disk and an HTTP client are the other two — and it adds no decode of
    32	its own. The response bodies embed entire-records' own DTOs rather than mirroring
    33	them, so the wire shape cannot drift from the decode that produces it. Nothing
    34	guards the *field set* against an upstream rename, though: the spec test pins the
    35	component names this service publishes, not their contents. That is a knowing gap
    36	while the surface is on v0 — see the consequences below.
    37	
    38	The dependency is pinned by pseudo-version on `main`. That repo has no tags and
    39	deliberately deferred extracting a tagged decode module, so this is what
    40	`entire-plans` already does. Go pins the commit, so an upstream change can only
    41	break the build of whoever bumps it.
    42	
    43	Three deliberate noes:
    44	
    45	**Read-only.** Writes need an atomic multi-record commit. The single-key writes
    46	git-meta offers today would leave a record observably half-written, which is worse
    47	than offering none.
    48	
    49	**No authorship, and no discards.** Both are derived by walking commit history.
    50	A schema that wants provenance declares stamped fields (`stamp: writeTime` /
    51	`writer`) and the answer arrives in the record's own fields at no cost, which is
    52	what the reference UI already does. This keeps a read O(store) rather than
    53	O(history) — and it leaves the wire shape untouched, so serving attribution later
    54	(from a push-fed table rather than a per-request walk) is purely additive against
    55	fields the contract already declares.
    56	
    57	**Lists paginate, and the array is named `items`.** The several-types-at-one-commit
    58	read returns a flat list rather than a map keyed by type: every record names its
    59	own type, so grouping is the client's to do, and a page of a map of arrays has no
    60	well-defined boundary. The page token carries the pinned commit and the scope, so
    61	a continuation reads the tree its first page answered from. Paging bounds the
    62	response, not the upstream read — the store has no partial read, so a page still
    63	materialises the types it spans.
    64	
    65	**The imported types are published under this service's names.** Response bodies
    66	embed entire-records' DTOs, but a custom huma schema namer renames the whole
    67	graph (`RecordDTO` → `RecordsRecord`). Declaring local mirrors would have been a
    68	second statement of the wire shape — the thing most likely to drift — and a Go
    69	type alias would not work at all, since an alias is the same type and reflection
    70	still reports the original name. The gateway merges every cell service's spec into
    71	one document and renames collisions to `<upstream>__<name>`, so publishing a name
    72	as generic as `SchemaDTO` would let an unrelated service rename our clients' types.
    73	
    74	**Unsettled is a version, not a path segment.** The routes are served on the v0
    75	surface (`/api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records…`): a Huma API and OpenAPI document of
    76	their own, beside v1 rather than inside it, which the gateway serves at its v1
    77	base with the version swapped. A path segment saying "experimental" would have to
    78	change when the surface settles, and `api-review`'s VER-005 forbids it; VER-005
    79	allows "a real version", and v0 is one. Routes leave v0 by moving to v1 under the
    80	v1 rules, not by changing shape in place.
    81	
    82	*Amended 2026-10-01.* This originally said the caveat lived in an OpenAPI tag on
    83	the v1 document. A tag does not stop a client generating against the v1 document
    84	and binding to shapes that are still moving, and v1 only allows additive changes
    85	(VER-003). So the routes moved to v0 and left v1 without a deprecation window;
    86	`entire-plans`' published-plans worker was the only known caller.
    87	
    88	## Consequences
    89	
    90	- **This service is now a consumer of another repo's Go API**, and one with no
    91	  semver signal. What guards the seam is a set of unit tests over hand-built
    92	  stores: the two-method reader (warming, the segment-aligned covering filter,
    93	  failures not memoised as empty), the state conversion in both directions, and
    94	  the read scoping. What is NOT guarded is an upstream field rename reaching this
    95	  service's published spec — the check that would catch it is a byte-for-byte
    96	  comparison against a store decoded by a reader we already trust.
    97	- **That comparison was built and then removed, deliberately.** It existed
    98	  because entire-api and entire-records held two independently-written
    99	  implementations of the git-meta exchange format, meeting in one conversion
   100	  function; a real store captured both ways was the cheapest proof they agreed.
   101	  Those implementations are being merged, which removes the reason — and the
   102	  fixture cost 238 KB of another repo's live data to carry. For an experimental,
   103	  read-only surface that is the wrong trade. If this surface graduates before the
   104	  merge lands, the check to restore is a small generated store (not a captured
   105	  one), which would also cover the reference, nested and list-field shapes no
   106	  capture of the planning store ever did.
   107	- **A records read is more permissive about schema names than the raw git-meta
   108	  read**, which rejects the uppercase in a camelCase schema name. entire-records'
   109	  own name rule decides here, and it forbids dots and slashes, which is the
   110	  property the namespace rule exists to enforce.
   111	- **`?ref` is read as given**, so a pin taken from another store returns that
   112	  store's records decoded against that store's schema: the path says where a read
   113	  started, not what the pin contains. It cannot cross a repo — the pin must name a
   114	  commit in this one — and it is the same latitude `/meta/targets` already allows.
   115	
   116	## Amendment, 2026-10-10: reads come from strata
   117	
   118	entire-plans made strata the authority for its records and kept git-meta only as
   119	a mirror, and entire-api grew a strata write path. Serving reads from the mirror
   120	would answer from a copy that lags the store and, for anything written through
   121	entire-api, never receives it. So the records routes now read strata stores.
   122	
   123	**The seam moved, the rule did not.** entire-records still does every decode;
   124	what this service supplies is now a `store.Projection` — this cell's Postgres
   125	projection of the store (`internal/recordprojection`), read through
   126	`store.NewProjectionReader` — instead of a git-meta `store.Reader`. The git-meta
   127	snapshot reader and its warming are gone.
   128	
   129	**Every read catches up first, and nothing else does.** A read fetches the store
   130	over git as the caller, into memory, and ticks the projection from its cursor
   131	under a per-store advisory lock before answering. A write that has landed is
   132	therefore visible to the next read without a pin, and a store nobody has
   133	projected yet is bootstrapped by its first read.
   134	
   135	**Over git, not the repo API.** A strata log entry carries its payload in its
   136	commit message, and the repo API caps a message at 64 KiB in its JSON pages, so a
   137	store with one large entry could never be read through it. git has no such cap,
   138	and it is the transport the write path uses already. The background consumer
   139	that followed ref events went with the repo API reader: it read cert-only, and
   140	entiredb admits entire-api cert-only on the repo API but not for git fetches. A
   141	read pays the catch-up for writes since the last read; if that shows up in

1	# Records are read through entire-records' own decode
     2	
     3	Status: accepted, 2026-08-10; amended 2026-10-01 (records move to the v0 surface); amended 2026-10-10 (reads come from strata)
     4	
     5	## Context
     6	
     7	A repo can hold [entire-records](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-records)
     8	stores: schema-described structured data kept as git trees on
     9	`refs/meta/records/<schema>/main`. Until now this service served only the raw
    10	`(target, key, value)` triples, on `GET /repos/{id}/meta/targets`, leaving every
    11	consumer to decode them.
    12	
    13	Decoding is not a formatting step. The rules are not recoverable by looking at the
    14	data: a record's shard is a hash of its id rather than an id prefix, a field's
    15	`:type` and `:value` keys recombine into one value, keys no type declares are
    16	dropped, an absent set encodes as `[]` where an absent scalar encodes as `null`,
    17	and an ordered type's records are sorted by a rank field. A second implementation
    18	gets most of that right and produces plausible-looking wrong records — which is
    19	worse than failing.
    20	
    21	entire-records' ADR `20260803-records-become-a-cell-api-concept` decided the
    22	answer jointly with us: records become a concept of this service, and that repo
    23	supplies the decode as a library above a two-method read seam (`store.Reader`).
    24	entire.io's TypeScript app then fetches decoded records over one hop and contains
    25	no records logic, which is what "no Go in that app" was asking for.
    26	
    27	## Decision
    28	
    29	**`internal/records` implements those two methods over this cell's git data plane,
    30	and imports everything above them.** It is the third implementation of the seam —
    31	a clone on disk and an HTTP client are the other two — and it adds no decode of
    32	its own. The response bodies embed entire-records' own DTOs rather than mirroring
    33	them, so the wire shape cannot drift from the decode that produces it. Nothing
    34	guards the *field set* against an upstream rename, though: the spec test pins the
    35	component names this service publishes, not their contents. That is a knowing gap
    36	while the surface is on v0 — see the consequences below.
    37	
    38	The dependency is pinned by pseudo-version on `main`. That repo has no tags and
    39	deliberately deferred extracting a tagged decode module, so this is what
    40	`entire-plans` already does. Go pins the commit, so an upstream change can only
    41	break the build of whoever bumps it.
    42	
    43	Three deliberate noes:
    44	
    45	**Read-only.** Writes need an atomic multi-record commit. The single-key writes
    46	git-meta offers today would leave a record observably half-written, which is worse
    47	than offering none.
    48	
    49	**No authorship, and no discards.** Both are derived by walking commit history.
    50	A schema that wants provenance declares stamped fields (`stamp: writeTime` /
    51	`writer`) and the answer arrives in the record's own fields at no cost, which is
    52	what the reference UI already does. This keeps a read O(store) rather than
    53	O(history) — and it leaves the wire shape untouched, so serving attribution later
    54	(from a push-fed table rather than a per-request walk) is purely additive against
    55	fields the contract already declares.
    56	
    57	**Lists paginate, and the array is named `items`.** The several-types-at-one-commit
    58	read returns a flat list rather than a map keyed by type: every record names its
    59	own type, so grouping is the client's to do, and a page of a map of arrays has no
    60	well-defined boundary. The page token carries the pinned commit and the scope, so
    61	a continuation reads the tree its first page answered from. Paging bounds the
    62	response, not the upstream read — the store has no partial read, so a page still
    63	materialises the types it spans.
    64	
    65	**The imported types are published under this service's names.** Response bodies
    66	embed entire-records' DTOs, but a custom huma schema namer renames the whole
    67	graph (`RecordDTO` → `RecordsRecord`). Declaring local mirrors would have been a
    68	second statement of the wire shape — the thing most likely to drift — and a Go
    69	type alias would not work at all, since an alias is the same type and reflection
    70	still reports the original name. The gateway merges every cell service's spec into
    71	one document and renames collisions to `<upstream>__<name>`, so publishing a name
    72	as generic as `SchemaDTO` would let an unrelated service rename our clients' types.
    73	
    74	**Unsettled is a version, not a path segment.** The routes are served on the v0
    75	surface (`/api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records…`): a Huma API and OpenAPI document of
    76	their own, beside v1 rather than inside it, which the gateway serves at its v1
    77	base with the version swapped. A path segment saying "experimental" would have to
    78	change when the surface settles, and `api-review`'s VER-005 forbids it; VER-005
    79	allows "a real version", and v0 is one. Routes leave v0 by moving to v1 under the
    80	v1 rules, not by changing shape in place.
    81	
    82	*Amended 2026-10-01.* This originally said the caveat lived in an OpenAPI tag on
    83	the v1 document. A tag does not stop a client generating against the v1 document
    84	and binding to shapes that are still moving, and v1 only allows additive changes
    85	(VER-003). So the routes moved to v0 and left v1 without a deprecation window;
    86	`entire-plans`' published-plans worker was the only known caller.
    87	
    88	## Consequences
    89	
    90	- **This service is now a consumer of another repo's Go API**, and one with no
    91	  semver signal. What guards the seam is a set of unit tests over hand-built
    92	  stores: the two-method reader (warming, the segment-aligned covering filter,
    93	  failures not memoised as empty), the state conversion in both directions, and
    94	  the read scoping. What is NOT guarded is an upstream field rename reaching this
    95	  service's published spec — the check that would catch it is a byte-for-byte
    96	  comparison against a store decoded by a reader we already trust.
    97	- **That comparison was built and then removed, deliberately.** It existed
    98	  because entire-api and entire-records held two independently-written
    99	  implementations of the git-meta exchange format, meeting in one conversion

   106	  capture of the planning store ever did.

See [`checkpoint-analysis-disable.md`](runbooks/checkpoint-analysis-disable.md) (the two
flags), [`checkpoint-analysis-enqueue.md`](runbooks/checkpoint-analysis-enqueue.md) (manual
`enqueue-analysis`), and
[`checkpoint-analysis-usage-cap.md`](runbooks/checkpoint-analysis-usage-cap.md) (parking +
`replay-deferred-analysis`).

## Event-stream consumers

Projections from shared streams into local tables. All default off: each binds a
stream provisioned per cell during rollout, and `CreateOrUpdateConsumer` errors
if the stream is absent, so they stay opt-in until it exists.

| Consumer | Binary | Stream / subject | Purpose | Gate |
|----------|--------|------------------|---------|------|
| `activity-ingester` | repo-activity | `repo_refs_v1` | Classify ref events → enqueue index jobs | always on |
| `activity-consumer` | user-activity | `user_activity_v1` | Write `my_activity` from forwarded events | always on |
| `author-reattribute-consumer` | repo-activity | `resource_lifecycle_v1` / `github_handle.*`, `verified_email.*` | On identity events, re-attribute a late signup's historical rows + `/me` forward | `CONSUME_RESOURCE_LIFECYCLE` |
| `repo-lifecycle-consumer` | repo-activity | `resource_lifecycle_v1` / `repo.*` | `repo.created`/`.deleted` → seed/remove the `repos` row | `CONSUME_REPO_LIFECYCLE` |
| `mirror-lifecycle-consumer` | repo-activity | `resource_lifecycle_v1` / `mirror.*` | `mirror.created` → seed the new placement + push group settings to it | `CONSUME_MIRROR_LIFECYCLE` |
| `user-lifecycle-consumer` | user-activity | `resource_lifecycle_v1` / `user.*` | `user.deleted` → purge account rows from the user store | `CONSUME_USER_LIFECYCLE` |
| `github-meta-consumer` | repo-activity | `github_meta_v1` | GitHub display metadata → `github_repo_meta` | `CONSUME_GITHUB_META` |
| `github-pr-consumer` | repo-activity | `github_pr_v1` | GitHub PR metadata → `github_pull_request_meta` | `CONSUME_PULL_REQUESTS` |

## Runner worker (cmd/runner, ENT-1289)

A **dedicated deployment**, not repo-activity-hosted (design doc
`sdd/2026-07-20-runner-machine-design.md` §4, D-9): sandbox orchestration
(provision/prompt/poll/snapshot, run scheduling) is bursty and long-poll-heavy
and must fail-isolate from the product-critical index pipeline, the same
rationale the BoH ingress spec used for webhook storms. Wired at startup in
`internal/server` (`RunRunner`); the actual work mounts in `internal/runner.Run`.

With both gates below on, `internal/runner.Run` starts three durables on
`runner_work_v1`, each with its own worker pool (`internal/runner/consumer.go`).
`runner-provision-consumer` and `runner-poll-consumer` have unlimited broker
redelivery, because provision coordinates ownership and poll re-enqueues
itself. `runner-work-consumer` handles prompt and snapshot with bounded
redelivery. The worker refuses to start without NATS and the repo store. With
`RUNNER_SANDBOX_PROVIDER` unset it still consumes, but every provider call
fails with `ErrProviderNotConfigured` (`internal/runner/provider_unconfigured.go`).
Pool sizes come from `RUNNER_WORKER_CONCURRENCY`,
`RUNNER_PROVISION_CONCURRENCY` and `RUNNER_POLL_CONCURRENCY`.
`RUNNER_MAX_ACK_PENDING` (default 1024) caps in-flight messages per durable,
shared by every pod, so adding pods does not raise it. On shutdown each durable
waits `RUNNER_DRAIN_GRACE_SECONDS` (default 20) for in-flight handlers. A
message that exhausts its retries goes to `runner_work_dlq_v1`, a stream fleet
provisions, not this service (`internal/runner/consumer.go`).

`REAP_ORPHAN_SANDBOXES`. It needs a sandbox provider and `JURISDICTION`, and
with `ORPHAN_SANDBOX_OBSERVE_ONLY` (default true) it logs what it would reclaim
without deleting anything.

`PUBLISH_*` gate in this file.

content.content:
by every gate, and by the one destructive path: `/preferences/repos` re-asks a
denial at full consistency before pruning the stored preference, because that
`DELETE` is not self-correcting.
_Avoid_: calling this "eventually consistent authz" — the *error* posture is still
absolute, and only the deny direction is relaxed.

### Records

**Records schema**:
A named, versioned set of record types together with the records that conform to
them, stored as git trees on `refs/meta/records/<name>/main`. Its *identity is its
name*: the version counts the breaking changes it has survived, so "planning is at
v3, readable through the shapes it had at v1 and v2" is one schema, not three.
The version is a key inside the store, so reading it costs a read — which is why
`GET /api/v0/repos/{repo_id}/records/{schema}` reports it and the schemas listing, which reads no
commit at all, does not. Defined and owned by
[entire-records](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-records); this service only
reads it.
_Avoid_: using bare "schema" — in this repo that first means a Postgres schema
(`repo`, `usr`) or a JSON/OpenAPI schema. Say which.

**Published store**:
The records a push produced, at `refs/meta/records/<name>/main` — the only view a
reader without a clone can see, and the one this service serves. A clone also has
a *local store* (`refs/meta/records/local/…`, holding unpushed work) and a
remote-tracking cache; neither is ours, and a difference between them is a real
difference rather than a bug.
_Avoid_: "the records", unqualified — it hides which of the three you mean.

**Superseded schema**:
The shape a records schema had at an earlier version, kept inside the live store
at `superseded/<N>` so `<name>@<N>` can be answered by reading the *live records*
through it. A lens, not a second store — there is one set of records and one ref.
This service does not serve it: `<name>@<N>` is refused as an invalid request
(400, not 404 — the store is there, the addressing isn't).
_Avoid_: "archive", and `refs/meta/records/<name>/v<N>`. That was the previous
model — a frozen snapshot on a ref of its own — and entire-records collapsed it.
A `v<N>` ref found in a repo is history, not a store.

**Tip**:
The commit a read is pinned to. Not merely "the latest commit": a read that names
a tip asks for a *state*, and a read that doesn't asks for whatever is current as
each part of it happens to be answered. A records read reports its tip so the next
read can ask for the same state — two collections read a moment apart can
otherwise disagree about what exists.

**Records namespace**:
`records/<name>/main` — a records store's **namespace** in this service's sense:
the complete ref sub-path under the fixed `refs/meta/` root, live segment
included. entire-records measures the same path from `refs/` instead
(`meta/records`), so converting between the two is a step worth naming rather
than rediscovering.

## Example dialogue

> **Dev:** For `/repos/{id}/contributors`, where does the 403-vs-404 ordering live now?
>
> **Reviewer:** In the access gate, not the handler. `repoOp` attaches
> `requireRepoAccess`, which runs the AccessChecker decision first — deny is `403`,
> a SpiceDB error is `503` — and only then checks the repo exists in this region for
> the `404`. That's authz-before-existence: the handler never sees an unauthorized caller.
	// A phase spans three orders of magnitude more than a run does: a checkout
	// lands in well under a second where an agent session runs for hours. On
	// runScaleBuckets every sub-second phase would collapse into one bucket, so
	// the phase histogram gets its own floor.
	runmetrics.PhaseDurationMetric: {0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1200, 1800, 3600, 7200, 14400, 43200, 86400},
	// One provider round trip, not a run: milliseconds to a few seconds, so
	// this starts three decades below the phase buckets. The tail past 10s is
	// kept coarse — a poll that slow is a provider incident, and which bucket
	// it lands in changes nothing.
	runmetrics.PollDurationMetric: {0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60},
	// A push reaching a live records reader: tens to hundreds of milliseconds
	// when healthy, so the buckets are densest there. Past a few seconds the
	// ring was held up (an outbox wake missed, a lock queue), not slow.
	"records.ring_lag": {0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 15, 60},
	// Bytes, not seconds, but the SDK defaults fail it the same way: every
	// sandbox would land in the overflow bucket. Dense between 512 MiB and
	// 8 GiB, where sandbox sizes sit.
	runmetrics.RunMemoryPeakMetric: {64 << 20, 128 << 20, 256 << 20, 512 << 20, 768 << 20, 1 << 30, 1536 << 20, 2 << 30, 3 << 30, 4 << 30, 6 << 30, 8 << 30, 12 << 30, 16 << 30},
}

// latencyHistogramViews renders our latency histograms as custom explicit-bucket

content.content:
822	## The SQL read model
823	
824	Git is the source of truth and the transport; a relational database answers the
825	questions git cannot answer quickly. `examples/project/sqlite` is that read model, and the
826	reference for what one looks like.
827	
828	```
829	records project read.db
830	```
831	
832	```sql
833	SELECT type, id, field, CAST(value AS TEXT), lamport FROM visible;
834	```
835	
836	Two tables and a view. `field` holds every value with the stamp that decided it;
837	`floor` holds each record's delete floor; `visible` joins them, since a
838	whole-record delete hides fields below it without erasing them and a field written
839	above it is visible again. The cursor lives in the database and is committed in
840	the same transaction as the values it accounts for, so it can never run ahead of
841	them.
842	
843	**The stamp column is what makes this work.** Every write is a conditional upsert
844	against it, so the projection is order-insensitive, idempotent and crash-safe, and
845	can run at the tip of the log rather than waiting for the barrier — a late op with
846	a lower stamp is refused by exactly the comparison the fold would have applied.
847	A test asserts that a database built a piece at a time, across compaction and
848	pruning, is byte-for-byte the database you get by building it from nothing.
849	
850	**The guard differs by class**, and this is where the read model had a real bug.
851	"Higher stamp wins" is only the mutable rule: the mirrored class is ordered by
852	upstream's version token, so a syncer resuming after being offline wrote stale
853	state with a later stamp and won — the store and the database disagreed about the
854	current value. The rule is stated once now, as `record.Supersedes`, and translated
855	into SQL per class. A property test asserts this sink and the in-memory reference
856	land on the same state for the same ops, drawing from all three classes.
857	
858	It drives the `sqlite3` binary for the same reason we drive `git`: no
859	dependencies, no cgo. The cost is a subprocess, so everything batches — a whole
860	projection pass is one process reading one transaction from a pipe. If `sqlite3`
861	is not on `PATH`, that package's tests skip and the rest of the module is
862	unaffected.
863	
864	## How long until a write is readable
865	
866	`mise run latency`. Timed end to end — the write is not counted as visible until
867	the value is readable through the `visible` view a consumer queries, not when
868	`Apply` returns.
869	
870	| unfolded tail | commit | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
871	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
872	| 0 | 54.2ms | 18.2ms | 3.5ms | 82.1ms | 88.6ms |
873	| 200 | 55.7ms | 30.4ms | 3.9ms | 95.7ms | 102.2ms |
874	| 1,000 | 57.2ms | 78.1ms | 4.4ms | 145.8ms | 150.6ms |
875	
876	**The database is not the cost.** Writing the batch is 4ms of a 90ms round trip,
877	flat as the tail grows. What costs is git: one subprocess to commit and several
878	to read the log back.
879	
880	**Reading the feed is O(tail), not O(what is new.)** A pass reads every entry in
881	the unfolded log and then discards what the cursor has already seen, so `feed`
882	climbs 18ms → 78ms while the work being done stays one op. Pruning is therefore a
883	read-latency lever and not only a disk one — the tail is what a projector pays for
884	on every pass, whether or not anything in it is new. A reader that keeps nothing
885	between passes can pay for only what is new instead: `FeedSince` reads on from
886	where the last pass stopped, and `FetchFor` fetches no more than that needs
887	(ADR-0025).
888	
889	For a reader on another clone, which is what visibility means when git is the
890	transport:
891	
892	| commit | push | fetch | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |

## The SQL read model

Git is the source of truth and the transport; a relational database answers the
questions git cannot answer quickly. `examples/project/sqlite` is that read model, and the
reference for what one looks like.

```
records project read.db
```

```sql
SELECT type, id, field, CAST(value AS TEXT), lamport FROM visible;
```

Two tables and a view. `field` holds every value with the stamp that decided it;
`floor` holds each record's delete floor; `visible` joins them, since a
whole-record delete hides fields below it without erasing them and a field written
above it is visible again. The cursor lives in the database and is committed in
the same transaction as the values it accounts for, so it can never run ahead of
them.

**The stamp column is what makes this work.** Every write is a conditional upsert
against it, so the projection is order-insensitive, idempotent and crash-safe, and
can run at the tip of the log rather than waiting for the barrier — a late op with
a lower stamp is refused by exactly the comparison the fold would have applied.
A test asserts that a database built a piece at a time, across compaction and
pruning, is byte-for-byte the database you get by building it from nothing.

**The guard differs by class**, and this is where the read model had a real bug.
"Higher stamp wins" is only the mutable rule: the mirrored class is ordered by
upstream's version token, so a syncer resuming after being offline wrote stale
state with a later stamp and won — the store and the database disagreed about the
current value. The rule is stated once now, as `record.Supersedes`, and translated
into SQL per class. A property test asserts this sink and the in-memory reference
land on the same state for the same ops, drawing from all three classes.

It drives the `sqlite3` binary for the same reason we drive `git`: no
dependencies, no cgo. The cost is a subprocess, so everything batches — a whole
projection pass is one process reading one transaction from a pipe. If `sqlite3`
is not on `PATH`, that package's tests skip and the rest of the module is
unaffected.

## How long until a write is readable

`mise run latency`. Timed end to end — the write is not counted as visible until
the value is readable through the `visible` view a consumer queries, not when
`Apply` returns.

| unfolded tail | commit | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 54.2ms | 18.2ms | 3.5ms | 82.1ms | 88.6ms |
| 200 | 55.7ms | 30.4ms | 3.9ms | 95.7ms | 102.2ms |
| 1,000 | 57.2ms | 78.1ms | 4.4ms | 145.8ms | 150.6ms |

**The database is not the cost.** Writing the batch is 4ms of a 90ms round trip,
flat as the tail grows. What costs is git: one subprocess to commit and several
to read the log back.

**Reading the feed is O(tail), not O(what is new.)** A pass reads every entry in
the unfolded log and then discards what the cursor has already seen, so `feed`
climbs 18ms → 78ms while the work being done stays one op. Pruning is therefore a
read-latency lever and not only a disk one — the tail is what a projector pays for
on every pass, whether or not anything in it is new. A reader that keeps nothing
between passes can pay for only what is new instead: `FeedSince` reads on from
where the last pass stopped, and `FetchFor` fetches no more than that needs
(ADR-0025).

For a reader on another clone, which is what visibility means when git is the
transport:

| commit | push | fetch | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 55.6ms | 61.5ms | 43.8ms | 19.1ms | 3.7ms | 189.8ms | 201.1ms |

Three git round trips and a database write. The two halves belong to different
people: the writer decides when to push, the reader decides how often to fetch.

**Compaction used to spike it, twice over.** Publishing a generation puts the
cursor behind it, so the next pass carries a seed as well as ops. Writing this
gate found two separate reasons that cost more than it should.

The first was not about projection at all: reading a generation walked the shard
tree a level at a time, one subprocess per occupied shard — 141 of them at 200
records, 617ms to read what one recursive listing reads in 5. Every path that
opens a compacted store was paying it. It is one call now.

The second is the seed itself, and the fix is to stop re-reading what the
projection already has. A projection that consumed generation *n* holds everything
in it, so what it needs to reach *n+1* is the difference — and because an
unchanged record encodes to identical bytes and is therefore the same object, git
finds that difference without descending into a shard that did not move. Measured
at the same store state, against the same ops, feeding two cursors that differ
only in the generation they claim:

| records in the store | seed from the diff | seed the whole generation | records seeded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 200 | 43.0ms | 39.6ms | 128 vs 316 |
| 1,000 | 47.2ms | 52.0ms | 128 vs 1,084 |
| 4,000 | 46.5ms | 93.9ms | 128 vs 4,092 |
| 10,000 | 46.8ms | 177.3ms | 128 vs 10,108 |

**The diff is flat and the full seed is linear.** Below about 500 records the diff
is marginally slower — both paths cost the same two subprocesses, and at that size
the bytes are not what is expensive — so the crossover is around a thousand
records and the gap widens from there.

Reading the whole generation is still the right answer whenever this clone cannot
see where the projection was: a projection starting from nothing, or one so far
behind that the generation it last stood at has been retained away. Both fall back
to it, and a test asserts the two paths agree.

**What the store forgets, the projection forgets — but not by applying the
diff's deletions.** A record can leave a generation three ways, and they are not
the same event.

Expiry means the content is gone, and the read model has to follow or it grows
forever with no way to reconcile. It is carried as a Lamport cutoff per Type
rather than a list of what went, because a bare "remove this record" has no
stamp: this feed is unordered and can be redelivered, so an unguarded removal
would delete a value written after it. A cutoff cannot, it is idempotent, and the
full-seed path can state exactly the same cutoff — which is what keeps the two
paths in agreement. In SQL it is one `DELETE` rather than a row per record.

Roll-up is not a deletion at all. It replaces a closed writer's individual facts
with one bundle carrying the same bytes verbatim; nothing is lost, only
re-grained, and the read model keeps the fine grain on purpose. That is what makes

Erasure is the third, and it is the one that names its target — which is exactly
what the paragraph above says a projection cannot be handed. It escapes that for
one reason: an erasure carries a **bound**, and a value decided at or above it is
never covered. So re-applying an erasure after the value was rewritten leaves the
new value alone, which is the property the cutoff was invented for, obtained per
target instead of per type. The bound is what makes "remove this record" safe to
say; without it, it is not.

The set is restated on every batch rather than sent once, so a read model that
already held the value when the erasure was written loses it, and a projection
rebuilt from nothing lands in the same place as one that kept up. Both sinks apply
the same predicate — `wire.Erasure.Names` — rather than each forming an opinion
about which rows a target reaches, which is the fix for the bug this seam has
already had once.

1	# A follower may read on without the history behind it
     2	
     3	A Follower that is handed a **Since** — the commit each of the store's
     4	generations and each writer's newest log named when it last read, and the
     5	erasures in force then — reads only the entries written after it, and needs no
     6	other object. `FetchFor` says what to fetch for
     7	that read; `Follower.FeedSince` reads it and returns the next Since.
     8	
     9	## Context
    10	
    11	`Feed` is O(tail): it walks every live log from its tip to the root of its
    12	rotation, reads the newest generation's description, and restates the erasure set
    13	from both on every batch. On a clone that keeps its repository that is a cost in
    14	CPU. On a reader that keeps nothing between reads — entire-api's records
    15	projection opens an empty in-memory repository per tick and has its read model
    16	in Postgres — it is a cost in transfer: every tick that anything moved fetches
    17	the whole tail and the newest generation's tree to apply a handful of ops.
    18	
    19	What such a reader can keep is small: the tips it read, which git's fetch
    20	negotiation turns into "send me what is newer than these", and the erasure set,
    21	which is the one thing a batch restates that cannot be read from new entries.
    22	
    23	## Decision
    24	
    25	**A Since records what a feed reads, and nothing else.** The generations, and
    26	each writer's newest log. Announcements and evictions a feed reads only by name,
    27	and an older rotation is one a prune is still withdrawing; `Tips` leaves them
    28	out, and every party that compares a listing against a Since uses it.
    29	
    30	**A read goes on from a Since only across changes that add entries.** A log
    31	growing or a writer's first log appearing. A generation published, a log
    32	rotated, or a log or generation deleted by retirement or retention makes the
    33	read whole. Those are exactly the changes that discharge erasures,
    34	reseed a projection or drop entries, so between two incremental reads the
    35	erasure set only grows by what the new entries carry, and carrying it forward is
    36	exact rather than an approximation.
    37	
    38	**One function decides, for the fetch and for the read.** `FetchFor` applies it to
    39	what the remote advertises, `FeedSince` to the refs it was handed. A fetch that
    40	planned an incremental read and a read that went whole — or the reverse — is the
    41	failure this rules out.
    42	
    43	**It is Feed, over a survey told where to stop.** Reading on differs from a whole
    44	read in two answers only: the tail is read back to the Since's tips, and the
    45	erasures in force start from its set rather than the newest generation's. The
    46	survey takes the Since and gives those two answers; the batch is assembled by
    47	the same code either way.
    48	
    49	**Logs are walked by parent, not by Log.** `Reader.Log(tip)` returns everything
    50	reachable, and the commits before the stopping point are not held. `git.Commit`
    51	now carries its parents, and the incremental read walks first parents with
    52	`Commit` until it reaches the commit the Since names. On the git binary that is
    53	a process per new entry, which is the size of the tick. A log that does not reach
    54	back to it is `ErrNotIncremental`, never an answer from the entries it does
    55	hold; the caller reads whole.
    56	
    57	**An unchanged generation is not read.** Its erasures are already in the Since,
    58	and nothing else in a feed at a caught-up cursor needs it.
    59	
    60	**The Since sits beside the cursor, not inside it.** `project.Cursor` is how far a
    61	read model has consumed and means the same over any transport. A Since is where
    62	in a repository that consumption was read from.
    63	
    64	## Consequences
    65	
    66	- A reader that keeps nothing fetches, per tick, the new entries and nothing
    67	  else, and fetches whole around compaction and prune: never more than it did
    68	  before.
    69	- The reader keeps the Since durably with its cursor and in the same
    70	  transaction, so the two cannot describe different reads.
    71	- Every driver fills `Commit.Parents`. The conformance suite checks it against
    72	  `Log`.
    73	- `Feed` is unchanged and remains O(tail) for a clone that holds everything.
     1	# A store has one remote
     2	
     3	A store's remote is the remote whose fetch refspecs fetch the store. Once one
     4	does, `Configure` refuses any other name with `ErrSecondRemote`. The same name
     5	may still be pointed at a new URL. Other remotes in the repository, such as the
     6	code's own `origin` or `upstream`, are not the store's business and are not
     7	counted.
     8	
     9	## Context
    10	
    11	The API never said how many remotes a store could have. `Configure`, `Push`,
    12	`Fetch` and `Sync` all take a remote by name, tracking refs are laid out per
    13	remote, and capabilities are cached per remote. Nothing tested more than one,
    14	and the CLI configures only `origin`.
    15	
    16	Reviewing ADR-0026 found that a store with two remotes is unsafe in three ways,
    17	and two of them lose data silently:
    18	
    19	- **Retention** measured from the newest generation across every remote. A push
    20	  to the lagging remote could withdraw its newest generation while the
    21	  generation replacing it existed only on the other remote. That generation is
    22	  what the lagging remote's logs were pruned against.
    23	- **Prune** has the same flaw, and it was on `main` before ADR-0026. It prunes a
    24	  writer's log against the newest generation in the merged view. A push to a
    25	  remote that lacks that generation then publishes the pruned log without it.
    26	  Push never offers a generation this clone only holds as another remote's
    27	  tracking ref, so nothing brings the missing generation across.
    28	- **The push queue** is one per store. `Push(remote)` empties it, so a second
    29	  remote never receives the refs the first push took.
    30	
    31	All three have one cause: the survey reads `refs/strata-tracking/*` as a single
    32	view, and the queue does not know about remotes.
    33	
    34	## Decision
    35	
    36	**One remote per store, refused at `Configure`.** That makes all three hazards
    37	unreachable through the API, and it costs nothing today: the only user has one
    38	remote.
    39	
    40	**Retention guards per destination anyway.** `withdrawGenerations` withdraws a
    41	generation only from a remote whose listing holds a newer one (ADR-0026). It is
    42	cheap. It is also the right check even with one remote, because a remote's
    43	newest generation is the one thing retention must never take from it.
    44	
    45	**The remote is read from its refspec, not recorded.** The first version
    46	recorded the name under `strata.<store>.remote`. `git remote rename` left that
    47	naming a remote that no longer existed, and `Configure` then refused the new
    48	name for ever. Git carries a remote's refspecs through a rename, so reading
    49	them back cannot go stale. It also finds the remote for a clone configured
    50	before anything was recorded. Two remotes that both fetch the store can only
    51	come from configuration written by hand; they are refused, not chosen between.
    52	
    53	Announcing uses the same answer. It used to take the first remote `git remote`
    54	listed, which is sorted, so a code remote named `github` beside `origin` was
    55	fetched in place of the store's.
    56	
    57	A rename leaves two things behind, and both are left alone. The tracking refs
    58	stay under the old name, and the renamed remote's refspec still writes there
    59	when plain `git fetch` runs. Neither can lose data: both are older copies of
    60	the same remote, so neither holds a generation newer than the remote does.
    61	
    62	There is no check in `Open` and no status line. No store has two remotes yet,
    63	so there is nothing to detect, and refusing in `Open` could lock someone out of
    64	reading their own data.
    65	
    66	## Lifting it
    67	
    68	Several remotes need two things this design lacks:
    69	- a survey taken for a destination, which reads that remote's tracking refs and
    70	  the local ones and nothing else
    71	- a push queue per remote
    72	
    73	With both, Prune and Retain judge against what the destination holds, and every
    74	remote receives every ref. `Announce`, `Push`, `Fetch` and `Sync` already take a
    75	remote by name for that day. Until then, a second remote is a refusal.

    54	listed, which is sorted, so a code remote named `github` beside `origin` was
    55	fetched in place of the store's.
    56	
    57	A rename leaves two things behind, and both are left alone. The tracking refs
    58	stay under the old name, and the renamed remote's refspec still writes there
    59	when plain `git fetch` runs. Neither can lose data: both are older copies of
    60	the same remote, so neither holds a generation newer than the remote does.
    61	
    62	There is no check in `Open` and no status line. No store has two remotes yet,
    63	so there is nothing to detect, and refusing in `Open` could lock someone out of
    64	reading their own data.
    65	
    66	## Lifting it
    67	
    68	Several remotes need two things this design lacks:
    69	- a survey taken for a destination, which reads that remote's tracking refs and
    70	  the local ones and nothing else
    71	- a push queue per remote
    72	
    73	With both, Prune and Retain judge against what the destination holds, and every
    74	remote receives every ref. `Announce`, `Push`, `Fetch` and `Sync` already take a
    75	remote by name for that day. Until then, a second remote is a refusal.
