822	## The SQL read model
823	
824	Git is the source of truth and the transport; a relational database answers the
825	questions git cannot answer quickly. `examples/project/sqlite` is that read model, and the
826	reference for what one looks like.
827	
828	```
829	records project read.db
830	```
831	
832	```sql
833	SELECT type, id, field, CAST(value AS TEXT), lamport FROM visible;
834	```
835	
836	Two tables and a view. `field` holds every value with the stamp that decided it;
837	`floor` holds each record's delete floor; `visible` joins them, since a
838	whole-record delete hides fields below it without erasing them and a field written
839	above it is visible again. The cursor lives in the database and is committed in
840	the same transaction as the values it accounts for, so it can never run ahead of
841	them.
842	
843	**The stamp column is what makes this work.** Every write is a conditional upsert
844	against it, so the projection is order-insensitive, idempotent and crash-safe, and
845	can run at the tip of the log rather than waiting for the barrier — a late op with
846	a lower stamp is refused by exactly the comparison the fold would have applied.
847	A test asserts that a database built a piece at a time, across compaction and
848	pruning, is byte-for-byte the database you get by building it from nothing.
849	
850	**The guard differs by class**, and this is where the read model had a real bug.
851	"Higher stamp wins" is only the mutable rule: the mirrored class is ordered by
852	upstream's version token, so a syncer resuming after being offline wrote stale
853	state with a later stamp and won — the store and the database disagreed about the
854	current value. The rule is stated once now, as `record.Supersedes`, and translated
855	into SQL per class. A property test asserts this sink and the in-memory reference
856	land on the same state for the same ops, drawing from all three classes.
857	
858	It drives the `sqlite3` binary for the same reason we drive `git`: no
859	dependencies, no cgo. The cost is a subprocess, so everything batches — a whole
860	projection pass is one process reading one transaction from a pipe. If `sqlite3`
861	is not on `PATH`, that package's tests skip and the rest of the module is
862	unaffected.
863	
864	## How long until a write is readable
865	
866	`mise run latency`. Timed end to end — the write is not counted as visible until
867	the value is readable through the `visible` view a consumer queries, not when
868	`Apply` returns.
869	
870	| unfolded tail | commit | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
871	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
872	| 0 | 54.2ms | 18.2ms | 3.5ms | 82.1ms | 88.6ms |
873	| 200 | 55.7ms | 30.4ms | 3.9ms | 95.7ms | 102.2ms |
874	| 1,000 | 57.2ms | 78.1ms | 4.4ms | 145.8ms | 150.6ms |
875	
876	**The database is not the cost.** Writing the batch is 4ms of a 90ms round trip,
877	flat as the tail grows. What costs is git: one subprocess to commit and several
878	to read the log back.
879	
880	**Reading the feed is O(tail), not O(what is new.)** A pass reads every entry in
881	the unfolded log and then discards what the cursor has already seen, so `feed`
882	climbs 18ms → 78ms while the work being done stays one op. Pruning is therefore a
883	read-latency lever and not only a disk one — the tail is what a projector pays for
884	on every pass, whether or not anything in it is new. A reader that keeps nothing
885	between passes can pay for only what is new instead: `FeedSince` reads on from
886	where the last pass stopped, and `FetchFor` fetches no more than that needs
887	(ADR-0025).
888	
889	For a reader on another clone, which is what visibility means when git is the
890	transport:
891	
892	| commit | push | fetch | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
893	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
894	| 55.6ms | 61.5ms | 43.8ms | 19.1ms | 3.7ms | 189.8ms | 201.1ms |
895	
896	Three git round trips and a database write. The two halves belong to different
897	people: the writer decides when to push, the reader decides how often to fetch.
898	
899	**Compaction used to spike it, twice over.** Publishing a generation puts the
900	cursor behind it, so the next pass carries a seed as well as ops. Writing this
901	gate found two separate reasons that cost more than it should.
902	
903	The first was not about projection at all: reading a generation walked the shard
904	tree a level at a time, one subprocess per occupied shard — 141 of them at 200
905	records, 617ms to read what one recursive listing reads in 5. Every path that
906	opens a compacted store was paying it. It is one call now.
907	
908	The second is the seed itself, and the fix is to stop re-reading what the
909	projection already has. A projection that consumed generation *n* holds everything
910	in it, so what it needs to reach *n+1* is the difference — and because an
911	unchanged record encodes to identical bytes and is therefore the same object, git
912	finds that difference without descending into a shard that did not move. Measured
913	at the same store state, against the same ops, feeding two cursors that differ
914	only in the generation they claim:
915	
916	| records in the store | seed from the diff | seed the whole generation | records seeded |
917	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
918	| 200 | 43.0ms | 39.6ms | 128 vs 316 |
919	| 1,000 | 47.2ms | 52.0ms | 128 vs 1,084 |
920	| 4,000 | 46.5ms | 93.9ms | 128 vs 4,092 |
921	| 10,000 | 46.8ms | 177.3ms | 128 vs 10,108 |
922	
923	**The diff is flat and the full seed is linear.** Below about 500 records the diff
924	is marginally slower — both paths cost the same two subprocesses, and at that size
925	the bytes are not what is expensive — so the crossover is around a thousand
926	records and the gap widens from there.
927	
928	Reading the whole generation is still the right answer whenever this clone cannot
929	see where the projection was: a projection starting from nothing, or one so far
930	behind that the generation it last stood at has been retained away. Both fall back
931	to it, and a test asserts the two paths agree.
932	
933	**What the store forgets, the projection forgets — but not by applying the
934	diff's deletions.** A record can leave a generation three ways, and they are not
935	the same event.
936	
937	Expiry means the content is gone, and the read model has to follow or it grows
938	forever with no way to reconcile. It is carried as a Lamport cutoff per Type
939	rather than a list of what went, because a bare "remove this record" has no
940	stamp: this feed is unordered and can be redelivered, so an unguarded removal
941	would delete a value written after it. A cutoff cannot, it is idempotent, and the
942	full-seed path can state exactly the same cutoff — which is what keeps the two
943	paths in agreement. In SQL it is one `DELETE` rather than a row per record.
944	
945	Roll-up is not a deletion at all. It replaces a closed writer's individual facts
946	with one bundle carrying the same bytes verbatim; nothing is lost, only
947	re-grained, and the read model keeps the fine grain on purpose. That is what makes
948	recurrence queries answerable in SQL after the store has coarsened.
949	
950	Erasure is the third, and it is the one that names its target — which is exactly
951	what the paragraph above says a projection cannot be handed. It escapes that for
952	one reason: an erasure carries a **bound**, and a value decided at or above it is
953	never covered. So re-applying an erasure after the value was rewritten leaves the
954	new value alone, which is the property the cutoff was invented for, obtained per
955	target instead of per type. The bound is what makes "remove this record" safe to
956	say; without it, it is not.
957	
958	The set is restated on every batch rather than sent once, so a read model that
959	already held the value when the erasure was written loses it, and a projection
960	rebuilt from nothing lands in the same place as one that kept up. Both sinks apply
961	the same predicate — `wire.Erasure.Names` — rather than each forming an opinion
962	about which rows a target reaches, which is the fix for the bug this seam has
963	already had once.
964	
965	## Verifying a generation
966

1	# A follower may read on without the history behind it
     2	
     3	A Follower that is handed a **Since** — the commit each of the store's
     4	generations and each writer's newest log named when it last read, and the
     5	erasures in force then — reads only the entries written after it, and needs no
     6	other object. `FetchFor` says what to fetch for
     7	that read; `Follower.FeedSince` reads it and returns the next Since.
     8	
     9	## Context
    10	
    11	`Feed` is O(tail): it walks every live log from its tip to the root of its
    12	rotation, reads the newest generation's description, and restates the erasure set
    13	from both on every batch. On a clone that keeps its repository that is a cost in
    14	CPU. On a reader that keeps nothing between reads — entire-api's records
    15	projection opens an empty in-memory repository per tick and has its read model
    16	in Postgres — it is a cost in transfer: every tick that anything moved fetches
    17	the whole tail and the newest generation's tree to apply a handful of ops.
    18	
    19	What such a reader can keep is small: the tips it read, which git's fetch
    20	negotiation turns into "send me what is newer than these", and the erasure set,
    21	which is the one thing a batch restates that cannot be read from new entries.
    22	
    23	## Decision
    24	
    25	**A Since records what a feed reads, and nothing else.** The generations, and
    26	each writer's newest log. Announcements and evictions a feed reads only by name,
    27	and an older rotation is one a prune is still withdrawing; `Tips` leaves them
    28	out, and every party that compares a listing against a Since uses it.
    29	
    30	**A read goes on from a Since only across changes that add entries.** A log
    31	growing or a writer's first log appearing. A generation published, a log
    32	rotated, or a log or generation deleted by retirement or retention makes the
    33	read whole. Those are exactly the changes that discharge erasures,
    34	reseed a projection or drop entries, so between two incremental reads the
    35	erasure set only grows by what the new entries carry, and carrying it forward is
    36	exact rather than an approximation.
    37	
    38	**One function decides, for the fetch and for the read.** `FetchFor` applies it to
    39	what the remote advertises, `FeedSince` to the refs it was handed. A fetch that
    40	planned an incremental read and a read that went whole — or the reverse — is the
    41	failure this rules out.
    42	
    43	**It is Feed, over a survey told where to stop.** Reading on differs from a whole
    44	read in two answers only: the tail is read back to the Since's tips, and the
    45	erasures in force start from its set rather than the newest generation's. The
    46	survey takes the Since and gives those two answers; the batch is assembled by
    47	the same code either way.
    48	
    49	**Logs are walked by parent, not by Log.** `Reader.Log(tip)` returns everything
    50	reachable, and the commits before the stopping point are not held. `git.Commit`
    51	now carries its parents, and the incremental read walks first parents with
    52	`Commit` until it reaches the commit the Since names. On the git binary that is
    53	a process per new entry, which is the size of the tick. A log that does not reach
    54	back to it is `ErrNotIncremental`, never an answer from the entries it does
    55	hold; the caller reads whole.
    56	
    57	**An unchanged generation is not read.** Its erasures are already in the Since,
    58	and nothing else in a feed at a caught-up cursor needs it.
    59	
    60	**The Since sits beside the cursor, not inside it.** `project.Cursor` is how far a
    61	read model has consumed and means the same over any transport. A Since is where
    62	in a repository that consumption was read from.
    63	
    64	## Consequences
    65	
    66	- A reader that keeps nothing fetches, per tick, the new entries and nothing
    67	  else, and fetches whole around compaction and prune: never more than it did
    68	  before.
    69	- The reader keeps the Since durably with its cursor and in the same
    70	  transaction, so the two cannot describe different reads.
    71	- Every driver fills `Commit.Parents`. The conformance suite checks it against
    72	  `Log`.
    73	- `Feed` is unchanged and remains O(tail) for a clone that holds everything.
     1	# A store has one remote
     2	
     3	A store's remote is the remote whose fetch refspecs fetch the store. Once one
     4	does, `Configure` refuses any other name with `ErrSecondRemote`. The same name
     5	may still be pointed at a new URL. Other remotes in the repository, such as the
     6	code's own `origin` or `upstream`, are not the store's business and are not
     7	counted.
     8	
     9	## Context
    10	
    11	The API never said how many remotes a store could have. `Configure`, `Push`,
    12	`Fetch` and `Sync` all take a remote by name, tracking refs are laid out per
    13	remote, and capabilities are cached per remote. Nothing tested more than one,
    14	and the CLI configures only `origin`.
    15	
    16	Reviewing ADR-0026 found that a store with two remotes is unsafe in three ways,
    17	and two of them lose data silently:
    18	
    19	- **Retention** measured from the newest generation across every remote. A push
    20	  to the lagging remote could withdraw its newest generation while the
    21	  generation replacing it existed only on the other remote. That generation is
    22	  what the lagging remote's logs were pruned against.
    23	- **Prune** has the same flaw, and it was on `main` before ADR-0026. It prunes a
    24	  writer's log against the newest generation in the merged view. A push to a
    25	  remote that lacks that generation then publishes the pruned log without it.
    26	  Push never offers a generation this clone only holds as another remote's
    27	  tracking ref, so nothing brings the missing generation across.
    28	- **The push queue** is one per store. `Push(remote)` empties it, so a second
    29	  remote never receives the refs the first push took.
    30	
    31	All three have one cause: the survey reads `refs/strata-tracking/*` as a single
    32	view, and the queue does not know about remotes.
    33	
    34	## Decision
    35	
    36	**One remote per store, refused at `Configure`.** That makes all three hazards
    37	unreachable through the API, and it costs nothing today: the only user has one
    38	remote.
    39	
    40	**Retention guards per destination anyway.** `withdrawGenerations` withdraws a
    41	generation only from a remote whose listing holds a newer one (ADR-0026). It is
    42	cheap. It is also the right check even with one remote, because a remote's
    43	newest generation is the one thing retention must never take from it.
    44	
    45	**The remote is read from its refspec, not recorded.** The first version
    46	recorded the name under `strata.<store>.remote`. `git remote rename` left that
    47	naming a remote that no longer existed, and `Configure` then refused the new
    48	name for ever. Git carries a remote's refspecs through a rename, so reading
    49	them back cannot go stale. It also finds the remote for a clone configured
    50	before anything was recorded. Two remotes that both fetch the store can only
    51	come from configuration written by hand; they are refused, not chosen between.
    52	
    53	Announcing uses the same answer. It used to take the first remote `git remote`
    54	listed, which is sorted, so a code remote named `github` beside `origin` was
    55	fetched in place of the store's.
    56	
    57	A rename leaves two things behind, and both are left alone. The tracking refs
    58	stay under the old name, and the renamed remote's refspec still writes there
    59	when plain `git fetch` runs. Neither can lose data: both are older copies of
    60	the same remote, so neither holds a generation newer than the remote does.
    61	
    62	There is no check in `Open` and no status line. No store has two remotes yet,
    63	so there is nothing to detect, and refusing in `Open` could lock someone out of
    64	reading their own data.
    65	
    66	## Lifting it
    67	
    68	Several remotes need two things this design lacks:
    69	- a survey taken for a destination, which reads that remote's tracking refs and
    70	  the local ones and nothing else
    71	- a push queue per remote
    72	
    73	With both, Prune and Retain judge against what the destination holds, and every
    74	remote receives every ref. `Announce`, `Push`, `Fetch` and `Sync` already take a
    75	remote by name for that day. Until then, a second remote is a refusal.

1	// Command refevents measures how long a record takes to become readable in
2	// another clone, when the reader is woken by the remote's own ref-change events
3	// rather than by a poll.
4	//
5	// Two clones of one store, in one process, on opposite sides of the wire:
6	//
7	//	writer ──append──▶ local refs ──push──▶ remote ──ref event──▶ reader
8	//	                                          │                     │
9	//	                                          └───────fetch─────────┘
10	//
11	// The point is what the reader does *not* do. It never polls the remote on a
12	// timer, and it never reads a value out of an event. It waits to be told that
13	// something moved, then fetches and folds — so the stream is a latency
14	// optimisation over a correct-but-slow loop, not a source of truth. That is what
15	// lets it stay correct under a signal that coalesces bursts, replays no history,
16	// keeps no cursor, and re-snapshots on reconnect. See events.go.
17	//
18	// # How the number is arrived at
19	//
20	// The writer puts the time it is about to commit into the record itself; the
21	// reader subtracts that from the time the value became visible in its read
22	// model. Both readings come from one process on one machine, so the subtraction
23	// is a duration and not a comparison of two clocks — which is the only reason
24	// this is worth measuring this way. Split the two halves across machines and the
25	// number would be measuring NTP skew as much as anything else.
26	//
27	// What it therefore includes, end to end: a local commit, a push to the remote,
28	// the remote's own ref-event fan-out, the reader's fetch, and the fold into a
29	// read model. The second half of that — from being woken to the value being
30	// visible — is timed separately and reported alongside, because it is the half
31	// that is this library's to answer for. The rest is the network and the host.
32	//
33	// This is the remote sibling of `mise run latency`, which measures the same
34	// question without a wire: how long a write takes to become readable in SQL in
35	// the clone that wrote it.
36	//
37	// Run it against a real repository:
38	//
39	//	go run ./refevents \
40	//	  -repo et/your-org/your-repo \
41	//	  -remote entire://aws-ap-southeast-2.entire.io/et/your-org/your-repo \
42	//	  -token "$(entire auth token -j au)"
43	//
44	// It writes real records under refs/strata/<store>/ and prints what the reader
45	// sees. -clean removes them again on the way out.
46	package main
47	
48	import (
49		"context"
50		"encoding/json"
51		"errors"
52		"flag"
53		"fmt"
54		"log"
55		"net/http"
56		"net/url"
57		"os"
58		"os/signal"
59		"path/filepath"
60		"sort"
61		"strconv"
62		"strings"
63		"sync"
64		"syscall"
65		"time"
66	
67		"github.com/entirehq/strata/examples/gogit"
68		"github.com/entirehq/strata/git"
69		"github.com/entirehq/strata/gitbin"
70		"github.com/entirehq/strata/project"
71		"github.com/entirehq/strata/record"
72		"github.com/entirehq/strata/reflayout"
73		"github.com/entirehq/strata/settings"
74		"github.com/entirehq/strata/store"
75	)
76	
77	func main() {
78		var (
79			api      = flag.String("api", "https://aws-ap-southeast-2.api.entire.io/api/v1", "API root, including its version prefix")
80			repoPath = flag.String("repo", "", "repository path to resolve, e.g. et/org/name")
81			repoID   = flag.String("repo-id", "", "repository id, if you already have it (skips resolving)")
82			remote   = flag.String("remote", "", "git remote URL the writer pushes to")
83			token    = flag.String("token", os.Getenv("ENTIRE_TOKEN"), "bearer token; defaults to $ENTIRE_TOKEN")
84			name     = flag.String("store", "refevents", "store name, which decides the ref prefix")
85			every    = flag.Duration("every", 2*time.Second, "how often the writer appends and pushes")
86			rounds   = flag.Int("rounds", 5, "how many pushes the writer makes before stopping")
87			batch    = flag.Int("batch", 1, "records per push — the lever, since cost is per push and not per record")
88			clean    = flag.Bool("clean", true, "withdraw this store's refs from the remote on the way out")
89			via      = flag.String("transport", "gitbin", "how to reach the remote: gitbin (forks git) or gogit (in-process)")
90		)
91		flag.Parse()
92		if *remote == "" || *token == "" || (*repoPath == "" && *repoID == "") {
93			flag.Usage()
94			log.Fatal("need -remote, -token, and one of -repo or -repo-id")
95		}
96	
97		ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
98		defer stop()
99	
100		id := *repoID
101		if id == "" {
102			var err error
103			if id, err = resolve(ctx, *api, *token, *repoPath); err != nil {
104				log.Fatalf("resolving %s: %v", *repoPath, err)
105			}
106		}
107	
108		// The two transports do not dial the same URLs, and that is not an accident
109		// of configuration. entire:// is a remote-helper scheme — an instruction to
110		// run git-remote-entire, which only the git binary knows to do — so gogit
111		// needs the smart-HTTP endpoint that helper would have dialled, plus the
112		// credential it would have minted. See examples/gogit.
113		var tp git.Transport
114		switch *via {
115		case "gitbin":
116			tp = gitbin.Transport{}
117		case "gogit":
118			tp = gogit.Transport{Client: &http.Client{Transport: bearer{token: *token}}}
119		default:
120			log.Fatalf("unknown -transport %q; want gitbin or gogit", *via)
121		}
122	
123		dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "refevents-")
124		if err != nil {
125			log.Fatal(err)
126		}
127		defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
128	
129		// Two clones, because that is the interesting shape: the reader must learn
130		// about the writer's work the way any other clone would, through the remote.
131		// A store's refs live under one prefix, and reflayout is what says which —
132		// the same value the watcher filters the stream by, so the reader is woken
133		// for this store's pushes and nobody else's.
134		layout := reflayout.For(*name)
135		prefix := layout.Root().Prefix() + "/"
136	
137		writer, err := open(dir, "writer", *name, *remote, tp)
138		if err != nil {
139			log.Fatalf("writer: %v", err)
140		}
141		reader, err := open(dir, "reader", *name, *remote, tp)
142		if err != nil {
143			log.Fatalf("reader: %v", err)
144		}
145	
146		log.Printf("repo %s, store %q, watching %s, transport %s", id, *name, prefix, *via)
147	
148		var wg sync.WaitGroup
149		writing, cancelWriting := context.WithCancel(ctx)
150		defer cancelWriting()
151	
152		wg.Add(1)
153		go func() {
154			defer wg.Done()
155			defer cancelWriting()
156			if err := stream(writing, writer, *every, *rounds, *batch); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
157				log.Printf("writer: %v", err)
158			}
159		}()
160	
161		samples := make(chan sample, 1024)
162		var collected []sample
163		var collect sync.WaitGroup
164		collect.Add(1)
165		go func() {
166			defer collect.Done()
167			for s := range samples {
168				collected = append(collected, s)
169			}
170		}()
171	
172		wg.Add(1)
173		go func() {
174			defer wg.Done()
175			follow(writing, reader, Watcher{
176				BaseURL:  *api,
177				Token:    *token,
178				RepoID:   id,
179				Prefixes: []string{prefix},
180				// No client timeout: the stream is meant to stay open, and the
181				// context is what bounds it.
182				Client: &http.Client{},
183			}, samples)
184		}()
185	
186		wg.Wait()
187		collect.Wait()
188		report(collected)
189		if *clean {
190			withdraw(filepath.Join(dir, "writer"), layout, tp)
191		}
192	}

194	// open prepares one clone of the store, pointed at the remote.
195	func open(root, who, name, remote string, tp git.Transport) (*store.Store, error) {
196		dir := filepath.Join(root, who)
197		if err := os.MkdirAll(dir, 0o755); err != nil {
198			return nil, err
199		}
200		// The driver is the binary either way: every primitive a local repository
201		// needs — create-if-absent compare-and-swap, a real ref transaction — is one
202		// go-git's reference store does not offer. Only the wire is swappable, which
203		// is exactly the split docs/adr/0020 makes.
204		return store.Prepare(gitbin.Driver{}, tp, dir, name, settings.Settings{}, remote)
205	}

207	// bearer attaches the token to every request the transport makes.
208	type bearer struct{ token string }
209	
210	func (b bearer) RoundTrip(r *http.Request) (*http.Response, error) {
211		r = r.Clone(r.Context())
212		r.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+b.token)
213		return http.DefaultTransport.RoundTrip(r)
214	}

216	// stream is the writer: append a record, publish it, repeat.
217	//
218	// Nothing here knows the reader exists. A push is the only thing it does that
219	// anyone else can observe, which is the property the whole arrangement rests on.
220	// A push costs what a push costs, whatever it carries.
221	//
222	// One advertisement of every ref on the remote, one receive-pack, one packfile —
223	// and on a host that locks per repository for a create-bearing push, one
224	// acquisition of that lock. None of it divides by the number of records in the
225	// batch, which makes batch size the only lever there is. It is not connection
226	// reuse: a receive-pack session serves exactly one push and cannot be reused,
227	// so "several updates down one connection" already means "one push carrying
228	// several refs", which is what a batch is.
229	func stream(ctx context.Context, s *store.Store, every time.Duration, rounds, batch int) error {
230		tick := time.NewTicker(every)
231		defer tick.Stop()
232		for i := range rounds {
233			select {
234			case <-ctx.Done():
235				return ctx.Err()
236			case <-tick.C:
237			}
238			// One draft, every record in the batch: the whole batch is stamped at
239			// the same moment and lands in one commit and one push.
240			draft := s.Begin()
241			body := strconv.FormatInt(time.Now().UnixNano(), 10)
242			for b := range batch {
243				draft.Set("note", fmt.Sprintf("m%03d-%02d", i, b), "body", []byte(body))
244			}
245			if err := draft.Commit(); err != nil {
246				return fmt.Errorf("writing batch %d: %w", i, err)
247			}
248			if err := s.Push("origin"); err != nil {
249				return fmt.Errorf("publishing batch %d: %w", i, err)
250			}
251			log.Printf("writer  ── pushed %d record(s) in one push", batch)
252		}
253		// A moment for the last push's event to arrive before the reader is stopped.
254		select {
255		case <-ctx.Done():
256		case <-time.After(3 * time.Second):
257		}
258		return nil
259	}

261	// follow is the reader: wait to be told something moved, then go and look.
262	//
263	// The two halves are deliberately separate. Watch decides *when* to look and
264	// knows nothing about records; drain decides *what changed* and knows nothing
265	// about the stream. Neither reads a value out of an event.
266	func follow(ctx context.Context, s *store.Store, w Watcher, samples chan<- sample) {
267		sink := project.NewMemory()
268		var cursor project.Cursor
269		seen := map[record.Key]bool{}
270	
271		look := make(chan string, 1)
272		go func() {
273			_ = w.Watch(ctx, func(ev Event) {
274				what := ev.Name
275				if ev.RefName != "" {
276					what = fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", ev.RefOp, ev.RefName)
277				}
278				// Coalescing on purpose: several events while a fetch is in flight
279				// collapse into one more look, because looking twice for one push
280				// costs a round trip and tells you nothing new. It also means a
281				// sample's measured latency is never inflated by queueing behind a
282				// fetch that was already going to cover it.
283				select {
284				case look <- what:
285				default:
286				}
287			})
288		}()
289	
290		for {
291			select {
292			case <-ctx.Done():
293				close(samples)
294				return
295			case what := <-look:
296				woke := time.Now()
297				n, touched, err := drain(s, sink, &cursor)
298				visible := time.Now()
299				if err != nil {
300					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, but: %v", what, err)
301					continue
302				}
303				if n == 0 {
304					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, nothing new", what)
305					continue
306				}
307				fresh := 0
308				var slowest time.Duration
309				for _, k := range touched {
310					if seen[k] {
311						continue
312					}
313					v, ok := sink.Visible(k, "body")
314					if !ok {
315						continue
316					}
317					written, convErr := strconv.ParseInt(string(v.Bytes), 10, 64)
318					if convErr != nil {
319						continue
320					}
321					seen[k] = true
322					fresh++
323					total := visible.Sub(time.Unix(0, written))
324					samples <- sample{key: k, total: total, read: visible.Sub(woke)}
325					slowest = max(slowest, total)
326				}
327				switch {
328				case fresh == 0:
329					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, %d op(s), nothing newly visible", what, n)
330				default:
331					// One line per wake-up rather than per record: a batch of a
332					// hundred arrives together and shares a latency, so a line each
333					// would be a hundred copies of one fact.
334					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, %d record(s) readable, slowest %s (%s of that fetch+fold)",
335						what, fresh, slowest.Round(time.Millisecond), visible.Sub(woke).Round(time.Millisecond))
336				}
337			}
338		}
339	}

341	// sample is one record's journey, timed.
342	type sample struct {
343		key record.Key
344		// total is write to readable-elsewhere: commit, push, the host's ref-event
345		// fan-out, the fetch it triggered, and the fold.
346		total time.Duration
347		// read is the tail of that — from being woken to the value being visible —
348		// which is the part this library answers for rather than the network.
349		read time.Duration
350	}

352	// report prints the distribution, which is the output that matters. A mean would
353	// hide the thing worth knowing: this path has a floor set by a round trip and a
354	// tail set by whatever the host was doing at the time.
355	func report(samples []sample) {
356		if len(samples) == 0 {
357			log.Print("no samples: nothing became readable")
358			return
359		}
360		totals := make([]time.Duration, len(samples))
361		reads := make([]time.Duration, len(samples))
362		for i, s := range samples {
363			totals[i], reads[i] = s.total, s.read
364		}
365		sort.Slice(totals, func(i, j int) bool { return totals[i] < totals[j] })
366		sort.Slice(reads, func(i, j int) bool { return reads[i] < reads[j] })
367	
368		log.Printf("%d samples", len(samples))
369		log.Printf("  write ─▶ readable elsewhere   min %s  p50 %s  p95 %s  max %s",
370			ms(totals[0]), ms(pick(totals, 0.50)), ms(pick(totals, 0.95)), ms(totals[len(totals)-1]))
371		log.Printf("    of which fetch+fold         min %s  p50 %s  p95 %s  max %s",
372			ms(reads[0]), ms(pick(reads, 0.50)), ms(pick(reads, 0.95)), ms(reads[len(reads)-1]))
373	}
374	
375	// pick is the nearest-rank percentile of a sorted slice.
376	func pick(sorted []time.Duration, q float64) time.Duration {
377		if len(sorted) == 0 {
378			return 0
379		}
380		i := int(q * float64(len(sorted)))
381		if i >= len(sorted) {
382			i = len(sorted) - 1
383		}
384		return sorted[i]
385	}
386	
387	func ms(d time.Duration) string { return d.Round(time.Millisecond).String() }
388	
389	// drain fetches what the remote has and folds it into the read model.
390	//
391	// Looped until a batch moves nothing, because one wake-up may cover several
392	// pushes: the stream coalesces, and a fetch can land more than the event that
393	// prompted it was about. The cursor is what makes that safe to repeat.
394	//
395	// It returns the keys the batch touched, which is the only thing the caller
396	// needs in order to print what changed — and note where they come from: the
397	// batch, not the event.
398	func drain(s *store.Store, sink *project.Memory, cursor *project.Cursor) (int, []record.Key, error) {
399		if err := s.Fetch("origin"); err != nil {
400			return 0, nil, fmt.Errorf("fetch: %w", err)
401		}
402		applied := 0
403		seen := map[record.Key]bool{}
404		var touched []record.Key
405		note := func(k record.Key) {
406			if !seen[k] {
407				seen[k] = true
408				touched = append(touched, k)
409			}
410		}
411		for {
412			batch, err := s.Feed(*cursor)
413			if err != nil {
414				return applied, touched, fmt.Errorf("feed: %w", err)
415			}
416			next, err := project.Apply(sink, batch)
417			if err != nil {
418				return applied, touched, fmt.Errorf("apply: %w", err)
419			}
420			for _, op := range batch.Ops {
421				note(op.Key())
422			}
423			for _, sd := range batch.Seed {
424				note(sd.Key)
425			}
426			moved := len(batch.Ops) + len(batch.Seed)
427			applied += moved
428			*cursor = next
429			if moved == 0 {
430				return applied, touched, nil
431			}
432		}
433	}

435	// withdraw removes this store's refs from the remote, so a demo run leaves
436	// nothing behind.
437	//
438	// Straight through the transport seam rather than through the store, because
439	// this is not a store operation — retiring a writer is, and that is a different
440	// thing with a barrier to respect. What this wants is the plain wire verb, and
441	// git.Transport is where that lives. Publishing is <ref>:<ref> and withdrawing
442	// is the same string with the left side left off, which is precisely why Push
443	// takes two lists instead of composed refspecs.
444	func withdraw(dir string, layout reflayout.Layout, tp git.Transport) {
445		repo, err := gitbin.Open(dir)
446		if err != nil {
447			log.Printf("clean: %v", err)
448			return
449		}
450		refs, err := tp.LsRemote(repo, "origin", layout.Root().Prefix())
451		if err != nil {
452			log.Printf("clean: listing: %v", err)
453			return
454		}
455		doomed := make([]string, 0, len(refs))
456		for ref := range refs {
457			doomed = append(doomed, ref)
458		}
459		if len(doomed) == 0 {
460			return
461		}
462		if err := tp.Push(repo, "origin", nil, git.Unleased(doomed...)); err != nil {
463			log.Printf("clean: %v", err)
464			return
465		}
466		log.Printf("cleaned %d ref(s) from the remote", len(doomed))
467	}

469	// resolve turns a repository path into the id the event stream is keyed by.
470	func resolve(ctx context.Context, api, token, path string) (string, error) {
471		u := fmt.Sprintf("%s/git/repos/resolve?repoPath=%s", strings.TrimRight(api, "/"), url.QueryEscape(path))
472		req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
473		if err != nil {
474			return "", err
475		}
476		req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token)
477		resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
478		if err != nil {
479			return "", err
480		}
481		defer resp.Body.Close()
482		if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
483			return "", fmt.Errorf("resolve: %s", resp.Status)
484		}
485		var body struct {
486			RepoID string `json:"repoId"`
487		}
488		if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&body); err != nil {
489			return "", err
490		}
491		if body.RepoID == "" {
492			return "", fmt.Errorf("resolve: no repoId for %q", path)
493		}
494		return body.RepoID, nil
495	}

15	// A ref event is a doorbell, not a delivery.
16	//
17	// This is the whole design of the reader below, and it is what makes an
18	// at-most-once live signal enough. The stream promises very little: rapid
19	// updates to one ref are coalesced to at most one event every ~200ms, there is
20	// no history and no cursor, and a reconnect re-snapshots rather than catching up
21	// on what it missed. Every one of those would be a problem for a consumer that
22	// treated events as the data.
23	//
24	// None of them is a problem for a consumer that treats an event as "something
25	// moved, go and look". The refs on the remote are the truth; the event only says
26	// when it is worth paying for a fetch. Miss one and the next one still leads to
27	// the same fetch. Get two for one push and the second fetch finds nothing new.
28	// Reconnect and the snapshot frame is just another prompt to look.
29	//
30	// The alternative — reading refName/newTarget out of the payload and treating it
31	// as state — would inherit every one of the stream's weaknesses as a correctness
32	// bug, and would do it silently.
33	
34	// Event is one frame from the ref-event stream.
35	//
36	// Carried in full because it is useful to print, and deliberately not used to
37	// decide anything: see the note above. RefOp is also in the body rather than
38	// only in the SSE frame name, because the server substitutes a safe frame name
39	// for any op it does not recognise and keeps the real one here.
40	type Event struct {
41		Name string // the SSE frame name: snapshot, create, update, delete, ...
42	
43		RefName         string `json:"refName"`
44		RefOp           string `json:"refOp"`
45		OldTarget       string `json:"oldTarget"`
46		NewTarget       string `json:"newTarget"`
47		OldSymrefTarget string `json:"oldSymrefTarget"`
48		NewSymrefTarget string `json:"newSymrefTarget"`
49		PusherID        string `json:"pusherId"`
50		EventAt         string `json:"eventAt"`
51	
52		// Refs is the snapshot frame's body, sent once when a connection opens.
53		Refs []struct {
54			Name         string `json:"name"`
55			OID          string `json:"oid"`
56			SymrefTarget string `json:"symrefTarget"`
57		} `json:"refs"`
58	}

60	// Watcher subscribes to a repository's ref-event stream.
61	type Watcher struct {
62		// BaseURL is the API root, including its version prefix.
63		BaseURL string
64		Token   string
65		RepoID  string
66		// Prefixes filters the stream server-side, in the same dialect the ref
67		// listing takes. Worth setting: a repository's branches and tags move for
68		// reasons a record store does not care about, and every one of them would
69		// otherwise cost a wasted fetch.
70		Prefixes []string
71		// Client is optional; http.DefaultClient is used when nil. A long-lived
72		// stream wants no timeout on the client itself — bound it with the context.
73		Client *http.Client
74	}
75	
76	// Watch calls ring for every frame until ctx ends, reconnecting on its own.
77	//
78	// Reconnection is not error handling here, it is the normal path: the server
79	// closes a connection after a bounded lifetime and says so with a reconnect
80	// frame. Because the reader re-derives its state from the store rather than from
81	// the stream, a gap between connections costs nothing but latency.
82	func (w Watcher) Watch(ctx context.Context, ring func(Event)) error {
83		backoff := 250 * time.Millisecond
84		for ctx.Err() == nil {
85			err := w.connect(ctx, ring)
86			if ctx.Err() != nil {
87				return ctx.Err()
88			}
89			if err != nil {
90				// Ring anyway. A connection that dropped may have dropped mid-push,
91				// and the cheapest way to find out is to look rather than to reason
92				// about it.
93				ring(Event{Name: "reconnect"})
94			}
95			select {
96			case <-ctx.Done():
97				return ctx.Err()
98			case <-time.After(backoff):
99			}
100			if backoff < 5*time.Second {
101				backoff *= 2
102			}
103		}
104		return ctx.Err()
105	}
106	
107	func (w Watcher) connect(ctx context.Context, ring func(Event)) error {
108		q := url.Values{}
109		for _, p := range w.Prefixes {
110			q.Add("prefix", p)
111		}
112		endpoint := fmt.Sprintf("%s/repos/%s/refs/events", strings.TrimRight(w.BaseURL, "/"), url.PathEscape(w.RepoID))
113		if len(q) > 0 {
114			endpoint += "?" + q.Encode()
115		}
116		req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
117		if err != nil {
118			return err
119		}
120		req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+w.Token)
121		req.Header.Set("Accept", "text/event-stream")
122	
123		cl := w.Client
124		if cl == nil {
125			cl = http.DefaultClient
126		}
127		resp, err := cl.Do(req)
128		if err != nil {
129			return err
130		}
131		defer resp.Body.Close()
132		if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
133			body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 512))
134			return fmt.Errorf("refs/events: %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
135		}
136		return parse(resp.Body, ring)
137	}
138	
139	// parse reads server-sent events and calls ring once per complete frame.
140	//
141	// Only the two line kinds this stream uses are handled — "event:" and "data:" —
142	// plus comments, which is what the heartbeat is (": ping <millis>"). A blank
143	// line ends a frame. Anything else is skipped rather than refused: a stream that
144	// gained a field should not stop a reader that does not need it.
145	func parse(r io.Reader, ring func(Event)) error {
146		sc := bufio.NewScanner(r)
147		sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 4*1024*1024)
148		var name, data string
149		for sc.Scan() {
150			line := sc.Text()
151			switch {
152			case line == "":
153				if name != "" || data != "" {
154					ev := Event{Name: name}
155					if data != "" {
156						// A frame whose body will not parse is still a prompt to
157						// look, which is the one thing this reader needs from it.
158						_ = json.Unmarshal([]byte(data), &ev)
159					}
160					ring(ev)
161				}
162				name, data = "", ""
163			case strings.HasPrefix(line, ":"):
164				// A heartbeat. It proves the connection is alive and means nothing
165				// moved, so it is deliberately not a prompt to fetch.
166			case strings.HasPrefix(line, "event:"):
167				name = strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(line, "event:"))
168			case strings.HasPrefix(line, "data:"):
169				data += strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(line, "data:"))
170			}
171		}
172		return sc.Err()
173	}

1	// Command refevents measures how long a record takes to become readable in
2	// another clone, when the reader is woken by the remote's own ref-change events
3	// rather than by a poll.
4	//
5	// Two clones of one store, in one process, on opposite sides of the wire:
6	//
7	//	writer ──append──▶ local refs ──push──▶ remote ──ref event──▶ reader
8	//	                                          │                     │
9	//	                                          └───────fetch─────────┘
10	//
11	// The point is what the reader does *not* do. It never polls the remote on a
12	// timer, and it never reads a value out of an event. It waits to be told that
13	// something moved, then fetches and folds — so the stream is a latency
14	// optimisation over a correct-but-slow loop, not a source of truth. That is what
15	// lets it stay correct under a signal that coalesces bursts, replays no history,
16	// keeps no cursor, and re-snapshots on reconnect. See events.go.
17	//
18	// # How the number is arrived at
19	//
20	// The writer puts the time it is about to commit into the record itself; the
21	// reader subtracts that from the time the value became visible in its read
22	// model. Both readings come from one process on one machine, so the subtraction
23	// is a duration and not a comparison of two clocks — which is the only reason
24	// this is worth measuring this way. Split the two halves across machines and the
25	// number would be measuring NTP skew as much as anything else.
26	//
27	// What it therefore includes, end to end: a local commit, a push to the remote,
28	// the remote's own ref-event fan-out, the reader's fetch, and the fold into a
29	// read model. The second half of that — from being woken to the value being
30	// visible — is timed separately and reported alongside, because it is the half
31	// that is this library's to answer for. The rest is the network and the host.
32	//
33	// This is the remote sibling of `mise run latency`, which measures the same
34	// question without a wire: how long a write takes to become readable in SQL in
35	// the clone that wrote it.
36	//
37	// Run it against a real repository:
38	//
39	//	go run ./refevents \
40	//	  -repo et/your-org/your-repo \
41	//	  -remote entire://aws-ap-southeast-2.entire.io/et/your-org/your-repo \
42	//	  -token "$(entire auth token -j au)"
43	//
44	// It writes real records under refs/strata/<store>/ and prints what the reader
45	// sees. -clean removes them again on the way out.

79			api      = flag.String("api", "https://aws-ap-southeast-2.api.entire.io/api/v1", "API root, including its version prefix")
80			repoPath = flag.String("repo", "", "repository path to resolve, e.g. et/org/name")
81			repoID   = flag.String("repo-id", "", "repository id, if you already have it (skips resolving)")
82			remote   = flag.String("remote", "", "git remote URL the writer pushes to")
83			token    = flag.String("token", os.Getenv("ENTIRE_TOKEN"), "bearer token; defaults to $ENTIRE_TOKEN")
84			name     = flag.String("store", "refevents", "store name, which decides the ref prefix")
85			every    = flag.Duration("every", 2*time.Second, "how often the writer appends and pushes")
86			rounds   = flag.Int("rounds", 5, "how many pushes the writer makes before stopping")
87			batch    = flag.Int("batch", 1, "records per push — the lever, since cost is per push and not per record")
88			clean    = flag.Bool("clean", true, "withdraw this store's refs from the remote on the way out")
89			via      = flag.String("transport", "gitbin", "how to reach the remote: gitbin (forks git) or gogit (in-process)")
90		)
91		flag.Parse()
92		if *remote == "" || *token == "" || (*repoPath == "" && *repoID == "") {
93			flag.Usage()
94			log.Fatal("need -remote, -token, and one of -repo or -repo-id")
95		}
96	
97		ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
98		defer stop()
99	
100		id := *repoID
101		if id == "" {
102			var err error
103			if id, err = resolve(ctx, *api, *token, *repoPath); err != nil {
104				log.Fatalf("resolving %s: %v", *repoPath, err)
105			}
106		}
107	
108		// The two transports do not dial the same URLs, and that is not an accident
109		// of configuration. entire:// is a remote-helper scheme — an instruction to
110		// run git-remote-entire, which only the git binary knows to do — so gogit
111		// needs the smart-HTTP endpoint that helper would have dialled, plus the
112		// credential it would have minted. See examples/gogit.
113		var tp git.Transport
114		switch *via {
115		case "gitbin":
116			tp = gitbin.Transport{}
117		case "gogit":
118			tp = gogit.Transport{Client: &http.Client{Transport: bearer{token: *token}}}
119		default:
120			log.Fatalf("unknown -transport %q; want gitbin or gogit", *via)
121		}
122	
123		dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "refevents-")
124		if err != nil {
125			log.Fatal(err)
126		}
127		defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
128	
129		// Two clones, because that is the interesting shape: the reader must learn
130		// about the writer's work the way any other clone would, through the remote.
131		// A store's refs live under one prefix, and reflayout is what says which —
132		// the same value the watcher filters the stream by, so the reader is woken
133		// for this store's pushes and nobody else's.
134		layout := reflayout.For(*name)
135		prefix := layout.Root().Prefix() + "/"
136	
137		writer, err := open(dir, "writer", *name, *remote, tp)
138		if err != nil {
139			log.Fatalf("writer: %v", err)
140		}
141		reader, err := open(dir, "reader", *name, *remote, tp)
142		if err != nil {
143			log.Fatalf("reader: %v", err)
144		}
145	
146		log.Printf("repo %s, store %q, watching %s, transport %s", id, *name, prefix, *via)
147	
148		var wg sync.WaitGroup
149		writing, cancelWriting := context.WithCancel(ctx)
150		defer cancelWriting()
151	
152		wg.Add(1)
153		go func() {
154			defer wg.Done()
155			defer cancelWriting()
156			if err := stream(writing, writer, *every, *rounds, *batch); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
157				log.Printf("writer: %v", err)
158			}
159		}()
160	
161		samples := make(chan sample, 1024)
162		var collected []sample
163		var collect sync.WaitGroup
164		collect.Add(1)
165		go func() {
166			defer collect.Done()
167			for s := range samples {
168				collected = append(collected, s)
169			}
170		}()
171	
172		wg.Add(1)
173		go func() {
174			defer wg.Done()
175			follow(writing, reader, Watcher{
176				BaseURL:  *api,
177				Token:    *token,
178				RepoID:   id,
179				Prefixes: []string{prefix},
180				// No client timeout: the stream is meant to stay open, and the
181				// context is what bounds it.
182				Client: &http.Client{},
183			}, samples)
184		}()
185	
186		wg.Wait()
187		collect.Wait()
188		report(collected)
189		if *clean {
190			withdraw(filepath.Join(dir, "writer"), layout, tp)
191		}
192	}

194	// open prepares one clone of the store, pointed at the remote.
195	func open(root, who, name, remote string, tp git.Transport) (*store.Store, error) {
196		dir := filepath.Join(root, who)
197		if err := os.MkdirAll(dir, 0o755); err != nil {
198			return nil, err
199		}
200		// The driver is the binary either way: every primitive a local repository
201		// needs — create-if-absent compare-and-swap, a real ref transaction — is one
202		// go-git's reference store does not offer. Only the wire is swappable, which
203		// is exactly the split docs/adr/0020 makes.
204		return store.Prepare(gitbin.Driver{}, tp, dir, name, settings.Settings{}, remote)
205	}

207	// bearer attaches the token to every request the transport makes.
208	type bearer struct{ token string }
209	
210	func (b bearer) RoundTrip(r *http.Request) (*http.Response, error) {
211		r = r.Clone(r.Context())
212		r.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+b.token)
213		return http.DefaultTransport.RoundTrip(r)
214	}

216	// stream is the writer: append a record, publish it, repeat.
217	//
218	// Nothing here knows the reader exists. A push is the only thing it does that
219	// anyone else can observe, which is the property the whole arrangement rests on.
220	// A push costs what a push costs, whatever it carries.
221	//
222	// One advertisement of every ref on the remote, one receive-pack, one packfile —
223	// and on a host that locks per repository for a create-bearing push, one
224	// acquisition of that lock. None of it divides by the number of records in the
225	// batch, which makes batch size the only lever there is. It is not connection
226	// reuse: a receive-pack session serves exactly one push and cannot be reused,
227	// so "several updates down one connection" already means "one push carrying
228	// several refs", which is what a batch is.
229	func stream(ctx context.Context, s *store.Store, every time.Duration, rounds, batch int) error {
230		tick := time.NewTicker(every)
231		defer tick.Stop()
232		for i := range rounds {
233			select {
234			case <-ctx.Done():
235				return ctx.Err()
236			case <-tick.C:
237			}
238			// One draft, every record in the batch: the whole batch is stamped at
239			// the same moment and lands in one commit and one push.
240			draft := s.Begin()
241			body := strconv.FormatInt(time.Now().UnixNano(), 10)
242			for b := range batch {
243				draft.Set("note", fmt.Sprintf("m%03d-%02d", i, b), "body", []byte(body))
244			}
245			if err := draft.Commit(); err != nil {
246				return fmt.Errorf("writing batch %d: %w", i, err)
247			}
248			if err := s.Push("origin"); err != nil {
249				return fmt.Errorf("publishing batch %d: %w", i, err)
250			}
251			log.Printf("writer  ── pushed %d record(s) in one push", batch)
252		}
253		// A moment for the last push's event to arrive before the reader is stopped.
254		select {
255		case <-ctx.Done():
256		case <-time.After(3 * time.Second):
257		}
258		return nil
259	}
260	
261	// follow is the reader: wait to be told something moved, then go and look.
262	//
263	// The two halves are deliberately separate. Watch decides *when* to look and
264	// knows nothing about records; drain decides *what changed* and knows nothing
265	// about the stream. Neither reads a value out of an event.
266	func follow(ctx context.Context, s *store.Store, w Watcher, samples chan<- sample) {
267		sink := project.NewMemory()
268		var cursor project.Cursor
269		seen := map[record.Key]bool{}
270	
271		look := make(chan string, 1)
272		go func() {
273			_ = w.Watch(ctx, func(ev Event) {
274				what := ev.Name
275				if ev.RefName != "" {
276					what = fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", ev.RefOp, ev.RefName)
277				}
278				// Coalescing on purpose: several events while a fetch is in flight
279				// collapse into one more look, because looking twice for one push
280				// costs a round trip and tells you nothing new. It also means a
281				// sample's measured latency is never inflated by queueing behind a
282				// fetch that was already going to cover it.
283				select {
284				case look <- what:
285				default:
286				}
287			})
288		}()
289	
290		for {
291			select {
292			case <-ctx.Done():
293				close(samples)
294				return
295			case what := <-look:
296				woke := time.Now()
297				n, touched, err := drain(s, sink, &cursor)
298				visible := time.Now()
299				if err != nil {
300					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, but: %v", what, err)
301					continue
302				}
303				if n == 0 {
304					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, nothing new", what)
305					continue
306				}
307				fresh := 0
308				var slowest time.Duration
309				for _, k := range touched {
310					if seen[k] {
311						continue
312					}
313					v, ok := sink.Visible(k, "body")
314					if !ok {
315						continue
316					}
317					written, convErr := strconv.ParseInt(string(v.Bytes), 10, 64)
318					if convErr != nil {
319						continue
320					}
321					seen[k] = true
322					fresh++
323					total := visible.Sub(time.Unix(0, written))
324					samples <- sample{key: k, total: total, read: visible.Sub(woke)}
325					slowest = max(slowest, total)
326				}
327				switch {
328				case fresh == 0:
329					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, %d op(s), nothing newly visible", what, n)
330				default:
331					// One line per wake-up rather than per record: a batch of a
332					// hundred arrives together and shares a latency, so a line each
333					// would be a hundred copies of one fact.
334					log.Printf("reader  ── woken by %s, %d record(s) readable, slowest %s (%s of that fetch+fold)",
335						what, fresh, slowest.Round(time.Millisecond), visible.Sub(woke).Round(time.Millisecond))
336				}
337			}
338		}
339	}

341	// sample is one record's journey, timed.
342	type sample struct {
343		key record.Key
344		// total is write to readable-elsewhere: commit, push, the host's ref-event
345		// fan-out, the fetch it triggered, and the fold.
346		total time.Duration
347		// read is the tail of that — from being woken to the value being visible —
348		// which is the part this library answers for rather than the network.
349		read time.Duration
350	}

352	// report prints the distribution, which is the output that matters. A mean would
353	// hide the thing worth knowing: this path has a floor set by a round trip and a
354	// tail set by whatever the host was doing at the time.
355	func report(samples []sample) {
356		if len(samples) == 0 {
357			log.Print("no samples: nothing became readable")
358			return
359		}
360		totals := make([]time.Duration, len(samples))
361		reads := make([]time.Duration, len(samples))
362		for i, s := range samples {
363			totals[i], reads[i] = s.total, s.read
364		}
365		sort.Slice(totals, func(i, j int) bool { return totals[i] < totals[j] })
366		sort.Slice(reads, func(i, j int) bool { return reads[i] < reads[j] })
367	
368		log.Printf("%d samples", len(samples))
369		log.Printf("  write ─▶ readable elsewhere   min %s  p50 %s  p95 %s  max %s",
370			ms(totals[0]), ms(pick(totals, 0.50)), ms(pick(totals, 0.95)), ms(totals[len(totals)-1]))
371		log.Printf("    of which fetch+fold         min %s  p50 %s  p95 %s  max %s",
372			ms(reads[0]), ms(pick(reads, 0.50)), ms(pick(reads, 0.95)), ms(reads[len(reads)-1]))
373	}
374	
375	// pick is the nearest-rank percentile of a sorted slice.
376	func pick(sorted []time.Duration, q float64) time.Duration {
377		if len(sorted) == 0 {
378			return 0
379		}
380		i := int(q * float64(len(sorted)))
381		if i >= len(sorted) {
382			i = len(sorted) - 1
383		}
384		return sorted[i]
385	}
386	
387	func ms(d time.Duration) string { return d.Round(time.Millisecond).String() }
388	
389	// drain fetches what the remote has and folds it into the read model.
390	//
391	// Looped until a batch moves nothing, because one wake-up may cover several
392	// pushes: the stream coalesces, and a fetch can land more than the event that
393	// prompted it was about. The cursor is what makes that safe to repeat.
394	//
395	// It returns the keys the batch touched, which is the only thing the caller
396	// needs in order to print what changed — and note where they come from: the
397	// batch, not the event.
398	func drain(s *store.Store, sink *project.Memory, cursor *project.Cursor) (int, []record.Key, error) {
399		if err := s.Fetch("origin"); err != nil {
400			return 0, nil, fmt.Errorf("fetch: %w", err)
401		}
402		applied := 0
403		seen := map[record.Key]bool{}
404		var touched []record.Key
405		note := func(k record.Key) {
406			if !seen[k] {
407				seen[k] = true
408				touched = append(touched, k)
409			}
410		}
411		for {
412			batch, err := s.Feed(*cursor)
413			if err != nil {
414				return applied, touched, fmt.Errorf("feed: %w", err)
415			}
416			next, err := project.Apply(sink, batch)
417			if err != nil {
418				return applied, touched, fmt.Errorf("apply: %w", err)
419			}
420			for _, op := range batch.Ops {
421				note(op.Key())
422			}
423			for _, sd := range batch.Seed {
424				note(sd.Key)
425			}
426			moved := len(batch.Ops) + len(batch.Seed)
427			applied += moved
428			*cursor = next
429			if moved == 0 {
430				return applied, touched, nil
431			}
432		}
433	}

435	// withdraw removes this store's refs from the remote, so a demo run leaves
436	// nothing behind.
437	//
438	// Straight through the transport seam rather than through the store, because
439	// this is not a store operation — retiring a writer is, and that is a different
440	// thing with a barrier to respect. What this wants is the plain wire verb, and
441	// git.Transport is where that lives. Publishing is <ref>:<ref> and withdrawing
442	// is the same string with the left side left off, which is precisely why Push
443	// takes two lists instead of composed refspecs.
444	func withdraw(dir string, layout reflayout.Layout, tp git.Transport) {
445		repo, err := gitbin.Open(dir)
446		if err != nil {
447			log.Printf("clean: %v", err)
448			return
449		}
450		refs, err := tp.LsRemote(repo, "origin", layout.Root().Prefix())
451		if err != nil {
452			log.Printf("clean: listing: %v", err)
453			return
454		}
455		doomed := make([]string, 0, len(refs))
456		for ref := range refs {
457			doomed = append(doomed, ref)
458		}
459		if len(doomed) == 0 {
460			return
461		}
462		if err := tp.Push(repo, "origin", nil, git.Unleased(doomed...)); err != nil {
463			log.Printf("clean: %v", err)
464			return
465		}
466		log.Printf("cleaned %d ref(s) from the remote", len(doomed))
467	}

469	// resolve turns a repository path into the id the event stream is keyed by.
470	func resolve(ctx context.Context, api, token, path string) (string, error) {
471		u := fmt.Sprintf("%s/git/repos/resolve?repoPath=%s", strings.TrimRight(api, "/"), url.QueryEscape(path))
472		req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
473		if err != nil {
474			return "", err
475		}
476		req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token)
477		resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
478		if err != nil {
479			return "", err
480		}
481		defer resp.Body.Close()
482		if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
483			return "", fmt.Errorf("resolve: %s", resp.Status)
484		}
485		var body struct {
486			RepoID string `json:"repoId"`
487		}
488		if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&body); err != nil {
489			return "", err
490		}
491		if body.RepoID == "" {
492			return "", fmt.Errorf("resolve: no repoId for %q", path)
493		}
494		return body.RepoID, nil
495	}

15	// A ref event is a doorbell, not a delivery.
16	//
17	// This is the whole design of the reader below, and it is what makes an
18	// at-most-once live signal enough. The stream promises very little: rapid
19	// updates to one ref are coalesced to at most one event every ~200ms, there is
20	// no history and no cursor, and a reconnect re-snapshots rather than catching up
21	// on what it missed. Every one of those would be a problem for a consumer that
22	// treated events as the data.
23	//
24	// None of them is a problem for a consumer that treats an event as "something
25	// moved, go and look". The refs on the remote are the truth; the event only says
26	// when it is worth paying for a fetch. Miss one and the next one still leads to
27	// the same fetch. Get two for one push and the second fetch finds nothing new.
28	// Reconnect and the snapshot frame is just another prompt to look.
29	//
30	// The alternative — reading refName/newTarget out of the payload and treating it
31	// as state — would inherit every one of the stream's weaknesses as a correctness
32	// bug, and would do it silently.
33	
34	// Event is one frame from the ref-event stream.
35	//
36	// Carried in full because it is useful to print, and deliberately not used to
37	// decide anything: see the note above. RefOp is also in the body rather than
38	// only in the SSE frame name, because the server substitutes a safe frame name
39	// for any op it does not recognise and keeps the real one here.
40	type Event struct {
41		Name string // the SSE frame name: snapshot, create, update, delete, ...
42	
43		RefName         string `json:"refName"`
44		RefOp           string `json:"refOp"`
45		OldTarget       string `json:"oldTarget"`
46		NewTarget       string `json:"newTarget"`
47		OldSymrefTarget string `json:"oldSymrefTarget"`
48		NewSymrefTarget string `json:"newSymrefTarget"`
49		PusherID        string `json:"pusherId"`
50		EventAt         string `json:"eventAt"`
51	
52		// Refs is the snapshot frame's body, sent once when a connection opens.
53		Refs []struct {
54			Name         string `json:"name"`
55			OID          string `json:"oid"`
56			SymrefTarget string `json:"symrefTarget"`
57		} `json:"refs"`
58	}

60	// Watcher subscribes to a repository's ref-event stream.
61	type Watcher struct {
62		// BaseURL is the API root, including its version prefix.
63		BaseURL string
64		Token   string
65		RepoID  string
66		// Prefixes filters the stream server-side, in the same dialect the ref
67		// listing takes. Worth setting: a repository's branches and tags move for
68		// reasons a record store does not care about, and every one of them would
69		// otherwise cost a wasted fetch.
70		Prefixes []string
71		// Client is optional; http.DefaultClient is used when nil. A long-lived
72		// stream wants no timeout on the client itself — bound it with the context.
73		Client *http.Client
74	}
75	
76	// Watch calls ring for every frame until ctx ends, reconnecting on its own.
77	//
78	// Reconnection is not error handling here, it is the normal path: the server
79	// closes a connection after a bounded lifetime and says so with a reconnect
80	// frame. Because the reader re-derives its state from the store rather than from
81	// the stream, a gap between connections costs nothing but latency.
82	func (w Watcher) Watch(ctx context.Context, ring func(Event)) error {
83		backoff := 250 * time.Millisecond
84		for ctx.Err() == nil {
85			err := w.connect(ctx, ring)
86			if ctx.Err() != nil {
87				return ctx.Err()
88			}
89			if err != nil {
90				// Ring anyway. A connection that dropped may have dropped mid-push,
91				// and the cheapest way to find out is to look rather than to reason
92				// about it.
93				ring(Event{Name: "reconnect"})
94			}
95			select {
96			case <-ctx.Done():
97				return ctx.Err()
98			case <-time.After(backoff):
99			}
100			if backoff < 5*time.Second {
101				backoff *= 2
102			}
103		}
104		return ctx.Err()
105	}
106	
107	func (w Watcher) connect(ctx context.Context, ring func(Event)) error {
108		q := url.Values{}
109		for _, p := range w.Prefixes {
110			q.Add("prefix", p)
111		}
112		endpoint := fmt.Sprintf("%s/repos/%s/refs/events", strings.TrimRight(w.BaseURL, "/"), url.PathEscape(w.RepoID))
113		if len(q) > 0 {
114			endpoint += "?" + q.Encode()
115		}
116		req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
117		if err != nil {
118			return err
119		}
120		req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+w.Token)
121		req.Header.Set("Accept", "text/event-stream")
122	
123		cl := w.Client
124		if cl == nil {
125			cl = http.DefaultClient
126		}
127		resp, err := cl.Do(req)
128		if err != nil {
129			return err
130		}
131		defer resp.Body.Close()
132		if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
133			body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 512))
134			return fmt.Errorf("refs/events: %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
135		}
136		return parse(resp.Body, ring)
137	}
138	
139	// parse reads server-sent events and calls ring once per complete frame.
140	//
141	// Only the two line kinds this stream uses are handled — "event:" and "data:" —
142	// plus comments, which is what the heartbeat is (": ping <millis>"). A blank
143	// line ends a frame. Anything else is skipped rather than refused: a stream that
144	// gained a field should not stop a reader that does not need it.
145	func parse(r io.Reader, ring func(Event)) error {
146		sc := bufio.NewScanner(r)
147		sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 4*1024*1024)
148		var name, data string
149		for sc.Scan() {
150			line := sc.Text()
151			switch {
152			case line == "":
153				if name != "" || data != "" {
154					ev := Event{Name: name}
155					if data != "" {
156						// A frame whose body will not parse is still a prompt to
157						// look, which is the one thing this reader needs from it.
158						_ = json.Unmarshal([]byte(data), &ev)
159					}
160					ring(ev)
161				}
162				name, data = "", ""
163			case strings.HasPrefix(line, ":"):
164				// A heartbeat. It proves the connection is alive and means nothing
165				// moved, so it is deliberately not a prompt to fetch.

1	# Push authorization is a server-side policy, not a log in the repository
     2	
     3	Write access to a repository is push access to every store in it. Git has no
     4	per-ref authorization, and nothing in this protocol changes that: a store's refs
     5	are ordinary refs. So the boundary a group actually gets is whatever the server
     6	enforces at receive time.
     7	
     8	We enforce it with a `pre-receive` hook (`cmd/strata-receive`) over a policy that
     9	lives on the server's disk, at `$GIT_DIR/strata-policy`. The decision itself is a
    10	pure function — `authz.Check(policy, identity, updates)` — with no git in it, so
    11	it is testable without a repository and the hook is a thin composition around it.
    12	
    13	A grant is per writer, not per store:
    14	
    15	```
    16	allow alice refs/strata/alpha/log/W1/*
    17	allow alice refs/strata/alpha/announced/W1
    18	allow alice refs/strata/alpha/gen/*
    19	```
    20	
    21	`authz.Grant` generates those three lines, because the ref layout is the
    22	protocol's business and a hand-written policy file is a second copy of it that
    23	diverges silently. The mistake worth designing out is a single
    24	`refs/strata/alpha/*` pattern: it hands every member every other member's log,
    25	and it looks reasonable.
    26	
    27	## Why not gittuf
    28	
    29	gittuf is the better answer to the part we have not solved. It has key
    30	distribution, rotation and revocation, and it keeps policy in the repository
    31	rather than in a forge, which is the stance this project takes everywhere else.
    32	
    33	It also records every reference update as an entry in one hash-chained log at
    34	`refs/gittuf/reference-state-log`. Every writer appends to that one ref and each
    35	entry names its predecessor, so concurrent appends cannot merge: a loser fetches,
    36	rebuilds and retries. Measured here (`mise run gittuf-cost`):
    37	
    38	| writers | appends | own refs refused | elapsed | attempts per append | gave up after 12 |
    39	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    40	| 4 | 20 | 0 | 4.3s | 2.5 | 0 |
    41	| 8 | 40 | 0 | 13.4s | 4.5 | 0 |
    42	| 16 | 80 | 0 | 43.1s | 7.4 | 9 |
    43	
    44	Eight writers pushing only their own refs, for comparison: 0.41s, nothing
    45	refused. This project exists
    46	because a shared-ref design collapsed under exactly that contention. Adopting one
    47	on the push path would undo its founding premise.
    48	
    49	Policy *in the repository* is separable from the RSL in principle, but not for
    50	free: it needs a trusted root to bootstrap from and a gated path for its own
    51	updates, which is most of what makes gittuf gittuf. A policy file on the server's
    52	disk needs neither, because it is not pushable. It is a smaller claim, and it is
    53	one that can be kept.
    54	
    55	## Consequences
    56	
    57	**The identity comes from the environment and never from the push.** The hook
    58	reads `STRATA_IDENTITY` (or the variable `STRATA_IDENTITY_VAR` names), which the
    59	server's access layer sets — an SSH forced command's record of which key
    60	authenticated, a proxy's authenticated user. Never a push option: those are sent
    61	by the client as part of the push being authorized, so an identity taken from one
    62	is a self-declaration. The same disqualifies the committer and author fields.
    63	
    64	**A missing policy denies.** A repository nobody configured fails on its first
    65	push rather than on its first incident.
    66	
    67	**A grant per writer could not express ending one.** Evict and Retire act on
    68	somebody else's refs, so the operational verbs this project ships could not be
    69	used against a deployment running the hook at all. The store-wide pattern refused
    70	above is now expressible with the dangerous verb withheld, which is
    71	[ADR-0015](0015-an-operator-grant-withholds-a-verb-rather-than-narrowing-a-pattern.md).
    72	The objection here stands: it is to what update permits, not to breadth.
    73	
    74	**`Grant` generated the lines and still fell behind the layout, so the layout
    75	moved.** Recorded here because this decision is where the reasoning was, and the
    76	reasoning was half applied. Generating the three lines removed one copy of the ref
    77	layout — the hand-written policy file — and left another: `authz` still named the
    78	kinds of ref itself, in `Grant` and again in the shape check. The layout then
    79	gained an eviction ref and `authz` did not hear about it, so `refs/strata/<store>/evicted/<writer>`
    80	was refused as an unknown kind, which is the push that releases the barrier
    81	(ADR-0002) — a one-shot writer could not close itself and compaction stopped. No
    82	test caught it because catching it needs the store's half and the hook's half in
    83	view at once, and no package held both. Both halves are now `reflayout`, which
    84	`store` and `authz` read; the grant is four lines; and an import-boundary test
    85	fails on any shipped code that spells a record ref out for itself.
    86	
    87	**A published generation may be created or deleted, never replaced** — for
    88	everyone, including an identity the policy trusts completely. Generations are
    89	verified by recomputation, which works only while the bytes at a number stay the
    90	bytes everyone folded. Replacing them leaves no evidence any later read could
    91	find: a clone that already adopted the old generation simply holds different data
    92	from one that adopts the new one, for ever. Creating and deleting are how
    93	generations are meant to move — published once, dropped by retention.
    94	
    95	**Refs the layout does not describe are refused** whatever the policy says. An
    96	unrecognised shape under `refs/strata/` is a mistake or an attempt.
    97	
    98	**A path remote authorizes nothing.** `git push /path/to/repo.git` runs
    99	`receive-pack` as a child of the pushing process, so the environment the hook sees
   100	is the pusher's. The hermetic tests here prove the hook — that the right refs are
   101	refused, that a refusal takes the whole push down, that a missing policy denies —
   102	and they prove nothing about authentication, which a path remote does not have.
   103	
   104	**This is not signing.** A signature says who wrote a value, survives compaction,
   105	and is checked by readers; it lives on the record and outside the protocol
   106	(ADR-0008). This says who may move a ref, is checked once by the server, and
   107	protects the parts of the layout no later reader could tell had been tampered
   108	with. Neither substitutes for the other.
     1	# A one-shot writer is authorised by shape, not by name
     2	
     3	A one-shot writer's identity is 130 bits of `crypto/rand` minted as it commits,
     4	and it must be: two processes that both claimed one identity would hand the same
     5	sequence number to different ops, and `(writer, seq)` is what ops deduplicate by —
     6	silent, permanent divergence. So the identity cannot be derived from a runner, a
     7	machine or a job, and no `authz` grant can name it in advance.
     8	
     9	The consequence was that CI reporting — the use case one-shot writers exist for
    10	([ADR-0002](0002-a-one-shot-writer-evicts-itself.md)) — worked against a path
    11	remote and against a server that authorises nothing, and not against one that
    12	does.
    13	
    14	## The rule
    15	
    16	A grant that names a store rather than a writer:
    17	
    18	```
    19	allow-oneshot ci refs/strata/alpha
    20	```
    21	
    22	It permits creating `announced/<W>`, `log/<W>/0` and `evicted/<W>` — all three,
    23	all as creations, for one `W`, with nothing else of that writer's in the push.
    24	That sentence is the glossary's definition of a **one-shot writer** ("creates
    25	its log, writes once, never appends, and evicts itself on completion") turned
    26	into a predicate, which is why the rule word names the term rather than coining
    27	one.
    28	
    29	It is decidable from the update set alone. A `pre-receive` hook runs once per push
    30	and is handed every ref it proposes, and `Check` already received them together —
    31	so this stays a pure function with no git in it, like the rest of the package.
    32	
    33	## Why the shape is enough
    34	
    35	Everything that keeps the grant narrow falls out of the shape rather than needing
    36	a check of its own:
    37	
    38	- **It cannot be grafted onto a writer that already exists.** That writer's
    39	  announcement is already on the server, so an update naming it is not a
    40	  creation, and the set is short. This is what a create-only grant over `log/*`
    41	  could not do: creating `log/<existing>/<n>` makes it that writer's log tip,
    42	  because a read takes the highest rotation.
    43	- **It cannot append later.** Rotation zero is named, and one ref arriving alone
    44	  is not a whole writer.
    45	- **It cannot introduce a writer that does not close itself.** The eviction is one
    46	  of the three, so ADR-0002's contract stops being a convention the client is
    47	  trusted to keep and becomes a condition of being let in. A writer admitted
    48	  without one would count toward the barrier for ever, and there would be no clone
    49	  left to evict it — the operator grant
    50	  ([ADR-0015](0015-an-operator-grant-withholds-a-verb-rather-than-narrowing-a-pattern.md))
    51	  can end a writer, but only one somebody knows about.
    52	
    53	## Considered options
    54	
    55	**Marking ephemeral writers in the ref layout**, so an ordinary prefix pattern
    56	could cover them. Conceptually simplest and needs no new rule shape. Rejected on
    57	cost and blast radius: eight sites in `reflayout` including `classify` and the
    58	store-name probe, `view.absorb`, `currentRotation`, `Retire`'s enumeration, and
    59	five pinning tests whose entire purpose is to make a change to ref *names* loud —
    60	because two clones on different builds meet on a remote that holds both.
    61	
    62	**A registration step**, where the runner asks the server for an identity first.
    63	Closest to how such systems usually work and it would make revocation possible.
    64	Rejected because it needs a service and a protocol where today there is a file on
    65	disk, which is most of what ADR-0012 chose a static policy to avoid.
    66	
    67	## Consequences
    68	
    69	**An identity holding this grant can create writers freely.** That is the
    70	capability, not a leak: a CI runner reports many runs and each is a writer. What
    71	it cannot do is touch a writer it did not create in that same push.
    72	
    73	**A one-shot writer now fetches before it announces.** It publishes a low-water
    74	mark — a promise never to write below a Lamport value — and a promise made
    75	against a view this clone has not refreshed promises something already false:
    76	the ops land below a boundary already folded, belong to no generation, and the
    77	next prune destroys them. [ADR-0009](0009-membership-must-be-announced.md) says
    78	announcing is where connectivity is required; this path returned before
    79	`mustBeAnnounced` and had no equivalent, so it never followed the rule that
    80	already covered it. It mattered little while a one-shot could not push to a
    81	guarded server at all. It matters now, and a CI runner is the likeliest clone in
    82	this design never to have fetched.
    83	
    84	**Writing is still offline for everyone else.** The fetch happens only where a
    85	remote is configured, and only on the path that announces.
